speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I beg to move, seconded by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll):
That the second report of the standing committee on industrial relations, presented on Tuesday, April 28, he now concurred in.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before this motion for concurrence in the second report of the standing committee on industrial relations is' carried, I should like to say just a few words. As hon. members are no doubt aware, the second report of this committee was tabled on Tuesday, April 28, and indicated that the committee had endorsed the principle of Bill No. 2 and recommended that the principle of the said bill, together with the submissions included in the printed evidence, be studied by the government in connection with its review and proposed revision of the provisions of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act.
No doubt hon. members are aware that Bill No. 2 is my bill which called for writing the check-off of trade union dues into the federal labour code. I certainly would not take the time of the house now to go into this matter at any length as it has been debated frequently in the house. Some of us would have liked to have seen progress made in the form of a legislative enactment at this session, but we are at least glad that this much progress has been made. After my bill having been defeated on several occasions, its principle has now been endorsed by the committee, and the motion now before us proposes that the house likewise endorse it and recommend to the government that the matter be studied.
I think attention should be drawn to the fact that the request for a study of this matter includes more than just what was in the bill. It asks the government also to study even more advanced ways of providing union security as suggested in some of the submissions included in the evidence that has been laid on the table of the house by the industrial relations committee.
As I say, some of us had hoped that we might get further than this at this session, but at least we are making progress. I trust that the study that will be made of this measure on the recommendation of the committee will result in some form of the checkoff being written into the federal labour code at the earliest possible date.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there was not a unanimous report of the committee in connection with this bill because I dissented and I refused to withdraw that dissent. I cannot understand the advantage of a voluntary revocable check-off because there is a certain contradiction in the term. Besides that, there are enough check-offs. There is a check-off for income tax, there is a check-off for something else, and there is a check-off for something else again. Now it is suggested there be a check-off for union dues which would benefit mostly the union leaders rather than the men.
If my hon. friends are in contact with the union leaders, I am in contact with the men. The men are fed up with these check-offs. They admit that there must be a check-off for income tax, but a check-off for this, a check-off for that, and a check-off to provide huge salaries for union leaders is more than enough. I am strongly opposed to it for the reasons I have mentioned.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not think the remarks of the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) can be allowed to stand as they are. As I understand it, the principle that was adopted by the industrial relations committee and which is now before us in its second report was the principle of a voluntary check-off. As far as this report is concerned, no member of a union will have his union dues taken off his pay cheque without his consent; and if he consents to do that, the next week decides that he does not wish to have it, he will withdraw his consent and there will be no further check-off so far as he is concerned. Things that are not correct should not be put on the record here, so as to stir up animosity between various groups and sections.
Motion agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: FIVE-DAY WEEK    REFERENCE TO STATEMENT IN PRESS
speechtext: I have not seen the statement, and I have no comment to make upon it.
The house resumed, from Monday, May 4, consideration of the motion of Mr. Fournier (Hull) for committee of supply, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Drew.

Mr. Speaker, I am going to refer first to the amendment before the house moved by the

Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) and seconded by myself, which reads:
That all the words after "That" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
whereas the natural resources of Canada are a heritage that should be developed and conserved for the purpose of providing the greatest possible measure of opportunity and security for all Canadians, this house is of the opinion that immediate consideration should be given to a national policy under a system of free enterprise and in close association and collaboration with the provinces that will:
(a)	promote and develop all the country's natural resources for the benefit of the people of every part of Canada;
(b)	protect and conserve our forest, mineral and other resources from undue depletion or exhaustion;
(c)	expand the use of our resources for industrial production in Canada and thus create greater opportunities for the employment, advancement and security of all Canadians.
I think the debate last night was an excellent one, and one in which the issues connected with this very important matter were placed before the house in a clear and definite manner by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in an address that covered the situation, and by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) in what, I must say, in its essence represented an outstanding contribution to the meaning and exposition of free enterprise.
Mention was made yesterday by one hon. member that we in Her Majesty's loyal opposition had only recently taken the stand of stating a policy in this connection. So that there will be no mistake in that regard I intend to read from a declaration on this matter by the Progressive Conservative party. Passed at a national convention, it indicates that since 1949, and prior to that date, the stand we have taken on this subject has been identical with that being taken today. I read:
The development of our natural resources upon the basis that they shall be processed in Canada will provide maximum employment and enable us to bring into Canada selected immigrants who will increase and give stability to our domestic market . . .
... in co-operation with the provinces to assist in the conservation and development of our natural resources and as one of the means to that end to establish a national development advisory council.
That is something, Mr. Speaker, that we Have advocated over and over again.
To institute in co-operation with the provinces a vigorous program of water conservation, reforestation, power development, flood control, comprehensive irrigation and drainage schemes for the reclamation of unproductive lands.
To establish a permanent program of maritime marshland reclamation.
To encourage and lend assistance in the production and marketing of maritime and western Canadian coal and the production of electric energy therefrom.
Natural Resources
To accelerate the development of our petroleum and other mineral resources in co-operation with the provinces by effective dominion-wide prospecting programs and by taxation and fiscal policies calculated to encourage the investment of risk capital.
Having said that, sir, I think the question of trade is of immense importance at this time as always. With the Prime Minister about to leave for Washington I feel that the house and the country would want him to know that, as the press says, one of his stands will be supported by Canadians generally-I refer to the question of the St. Lawrence waterway necessary to our national development. Also there is the need for the Prime Minister to make clear to the President of the United States that we in Canada feel that recent actions on the part of the United States government are interfering with trade and are a denial of the principles that were accepted by the United States, Canada and other nations in NATO. Such action is irksome to the Canadian people and is not in keeping with the responsibilities of NATO or of the nations in NATO. I refer particularly in that connection to the findings of the committee set up by President Truman in 1952 to report on a trade and tariff policy in the national interest. That committee made recommendations and those recommendations have been placed before congress by the executive in the manner provided by the American constitution. The recommendations made were as follows:
(1)	That a new simplified tariff act be adopted, providing for a general reduction of duties.
(2)	That tariffs be reduced, and quotas on agricultural products be liberalized to allow freer import of goods that are not produced in the United States in sufficient quantities at world prices.
(3)	That tariffs be reduced and in some cases ultimately eliminated on metals and minerals of which imports are a major part of U.S. supplies.
(4)	That the President be authorized to enter into reciprocal trade agreements without limit of time and with power to reduce tariffs, within specific limits, in return for reduction in tariffs or restrictions by other countries.
The representations made by that committee were in keeping with the general agreement on tariff and trade, and congress was asked to take the necessary steps to enable the United States to join in affording an opportunity, internationally, to promote the objectives of the Geneva agreement. Certainly what is happening today will have a most detrimental effect on Canada in the matter of production of minerals and also of agricultural products. If we in Canada are to take our place and make our contribution in the world today, that situation must be remedied. However much we may hope that the way of peace is present, the press reports of the last two or three days have not been optimistic about the probabilities

Natural Resources
that the U.S.S.R. has made a new move for peace. Rather, the indications are that she has made a detour and will return as in the past to the highways she has followed since 1921.
I feel that the Prime Minister, realizing how our export markets have been hit in the last three months, realizing the danger that Canada faces if the attitude being adopted by the United States of America on mineral imports is implemented, will know when he speaks in Washington that the stand he takes in order to remove these unfairnesses will have the support of the Canadian people generally.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member will allow me to say, in fairness, that I think we should attach some importance to the very strong arguments against these proposals which were put before the committee of congress yesterday by the secretary of state.

What the Prime Minister says is correct. Yesterday strong representations were made; but representations, having regard to the separation of the executive and the legislative bodies in the United States, are never as effective as they would be if the executive in the person of the President were in the position of the Prime Minister of Canada speaking to parliament.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I rose just because the hon. member was using the word "government" which, of course, can include the overall set-up but might have been understood to refer to the administration.

The Prime Minister has pointed out the distinction between the government in the United States and the government here. If there was any ambiguity in my remarks I am very happy that the Prime Minister cleared it away, because I had no intention of leaving the impression that the President of the United States and the secretary of state held any view different from the views expressed by other members of the NATO nations.
According to reports, what has taken place in congress in the last few days is not in keeping with that spirit of co-operation that one would expect. One congressman, a representative of the majority party in the United States, said:
Let Canada keep her nose out of our affairs.
It is not a question of Canada in any way endeavouring to interfere with the affairs of the United States; it is a question of joint survival in the world today. That cannot be achieved unless in the days of peace, from

the economic standpoint, we have the cooperation which we had in the days of war and in the days since the war. I feel that the trade situation is all part and parcel of the development of our resources. If we have not got trade channels, developed resources are meaningless.
I have here a Canadian Press report of April 29 pointing out that:
Canada's imports soared almost to the billion dollar mark in the first three months of 1953, but her exports dipped sharply, sweeping the foreign trade balance back into the deficit column.
It goes on to point out that Canada today, having regard to trade conditions generally in the world, is in the position that she is relying more and more on the United States market, partly because of her contiguity to the United States and partly as a result of the world situation.
I want to address myself now to a few remarks concerning our resources, and also to some suggestions as to the courses that I believe the government might direct itself towards in order to achieve the maximum development of the productive capacity of all the resources of Canada. We learned during the days of war that the state has a responsibility to foster an expanding economy. At the same time we learned that the commercial activities of the state, the industrial activities of the state, the development of our mines by the state cannot but be more costly than through the medium of free enterprise. I believe that in the world of today, if Canadians could catch a vision of the freedom of security we could enjoy in a real program of national development, Canadians would respond and develop measures to ensure and maintain a program of plenty.
In Saskatchewan we are enjoying today the development of our mineral and petroleum resources to an outstanding degree. We do not lose sight of the fact that these developments came about in the general developments taking place by reason of the demands of defence, and as a result also of the government of Saskatchewan departing from its principle that the state could best develop resources and returning to the encouragement of free enterprise to come into our province. I believe that free men can produce more than men directed by the state, and that our resources will not be developed with the state in the position of dictator or enterpriser. They will be developed in co-operation between the state and the giving of free enterprise and equal opportunity. This has within it the germ of the idea that the state must protect the weak

as against the strong, protect the small enterpriser as against the powerful who would illegally take advantage. The state has a responsibility to provide a national opportunity and the means; the individual must supply the initiative, the capacity, the ability and the foresight and also the realization that in all business there is profit and there is loss.
I have a few suggestions to offer in regard to the situation generally in the western provinces. Last evening the Prime Minister returned once more to the South Saskatchewan river project as a result of a question asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). He returned to that question and dealt with it on the basis of one of those things that might be contemplated in a great national development policy, provided the economics of that transaction were in keeping with the national return. In Saskatchewan today we find ourselves in the position that-this applies to the western provinces generally, whatever the denial may be-we have enjoyed little, proportionately, of the economic advantages that came to other parts of this country in connection with industrial and defence activities or those things incidental to the preparation for defence at this time.
Those of you who have never seen northern Saskatchewan have no conception of the vast potentialities there in uranium. I am not going into that now, as I have done so before. We have at Beaverlodge today a uranium area which is becoming the Mecca of prospectors from every part of the world. We live on the edge of the atomic power age. Chalk River has made possible a vast store of knowledge for commercial purposes. According to the estimates of the scientists, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) joined in those estimates, within five or six years there may be commercial production within this country as a consequence of the atomic development and the fission of the atom. The potentialities are tremendous. The challenge to us to use these potentialities is as great as the potentialities.
Canada has produced cobalt bombs, some six of them up until March 30, which were sold at $50,000 each to hospitals in Canada and the United States. The demand for these bombs is almost inexhaustible, and that indicates the advance that has been made since the beginning of the war. These cobalt bombs would have cost $50 million each had they been produced prior to the war.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
A victory for public enterprise.
Natural Resources

A victory for the
research activities on the part of public enterprise, making available those things and giving an opportunity to private enterprise to expand and develop them. As the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) mentioned yesterday, the state has a responsibility. When the minister speaks about a victory for public enterprise, I know of no one who, in his own life, represents more the activities of private enterprise and all it means and the benefits that it extends. But public enterprise has a field, as the Leader of the Opposition said last night, in connection with these natural monopolies that could not have been developed by private enterprise and would not have been developed by public enterprise if it had not been for the demands of war and the exigencies of the needs of world defence. We were forced into a position of developing those potentialities. It is one of the few benefits that come out of war. The research activities of the state ultimately become the advantages of the citizens of the state when the danger of war is past or when hostilities end.
In the development of the western provinces, we feel that certain things should be done in order to give us the dynamic and expanding economy, and in order to produce and develop our heritage as that heritage has been developed in other parts of the country. We feel that in the national interest, having regard to the tremendous cost of getting minerals out of the north, the transportation facilities should be made available by the state, and that there should be, in co-operation between the dominion and the provinces, a program to make available to private enterprise that north area which otherwise will not enjoy the development it should. We believe that in cooperation with the province there should be established a national development advisory council, to the end that an opportunity for development would be achieved which otherwise would be denied.
I mention railroads in northern Manitoba. The Canadian National rail link which begins at Sherridon and heads north to Lynn Lake, is one that has made available a new area and has also made possible maximum production by Sherritt-Gordon.
I mentioned uranium in the north, and I am not going to say any more about that matter; but I point out this consideration. Surely we in the prairie provinces have the right

and I again borrow the expression of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe)-to have the state render the opportunity for a western industrial development

Natural Resources
that we have not hitherto had. We have on the western plains today five sources of energy; coal, uranium, electric power, petroleum and natural gas. All we require is the development of the vast power resources that are in that province on the Churchill river, at Fort a la Come on the Saskatchewan river and again in connection with the South Saskatchewan river dam and development, in order to permit the industrialization which only power will make possible.
Then in a national development policy I believe we must realize the fact that taxation today is too high and denies to development that encouragement which it should receive. Someone may challenge that statement but, as a matter of fact, only recently Mr. Maxwell W. Mackenzie, who was formerly deputy minister of the Department of Trade and Commerce, spoke on this subject on or about March 10 in British Columbia where he now occupies the position of executive vice-president of one of the great commercial institutions in this country, and he said that taxation must not be allowed to kill the goose that lays the golden egg. Then he went on to say that the current level of taxation in Canada is certainly not much encouragement to the risk of large amounts of capital in new resource development. Those are not my words; those are the words of a man who for years was a civil servant of great distinction in the Department of Trade and Commerce and who now, viewing the matter from an objective angle, realizes that in this national development taxation must be maintained at a lower level. To that end-I add these words by way of my own observation-wasteful expenditures should be eliminated, for, without their elimination, there can be no reduction in taxation.
Then in that national development plan I believe that we in the prairie provinces-and I refer particularly to Alberta, Saskatchewan and the western part of Manitoba-have just reason to ask that, in pursuance of our defence activities, the federal government should assist the provinces in the building of defence roads. A road into northern Saskatchewan beyond the area of present settlement would be a defence road. It would make available less costly transportation of the minerals being produced in the north. In the event that war should come, it would also be available as a means of ingress and egress from the north, from those uranium areas which are becoming more and more extensive as the months go by. We feel that this is a matter of national importance. Those roads can be used today in 
order to permit of northern development. The concept is in keeping with the idea that the state gives the opportunity while allowing private enterprise generally to develop where equality of those opportunities shall be assured. At the same time we in the western provinces would harve available to us roads that could be used in defence if and when the need arises. In any event, having regard to the establishment of the camp at Wain-wright and the one at Dundurn, the highways are used in large measure by the heavy transport of the armed forces. I think the belief generally held by the people of our western provinces is that we have a right to ask for federal assistance in these works which, after all, are part and parcel of the defence of Canada.
There were other matters, Mr. Speaker, to which I could have referred but I wanted to place generally before the house some of the views that I believe are held in the western provinces by people of all political faiths. We believe that we in northern Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta stand at the threshold of the greatest and most revolutionary change that has ever taken place in the lifetime of any country. Today the United States of America is a "have-not" country with respect to minerals, petroleum and the like. She still has petroleum but her available resources are only 7i billion barrels more than is our potential in Canada. Her minerals have been spread over Europe and Asia during two world wars.	Our
minerals are in the virgin state of development. They are needed in mobilizing the forces of freedom everywhere. Undeveloped resources being ineffective for defence, we feel that the time has come for a national policy that will render those resources available for Canadians and for the people of every one of the United Nations and which will assure that development which heretofore we have envisioned and of which we are now on the threshold.
I do not believe in a nationalistic policy, Mr. Speaker; but I cannot conceive of Canada, with her vast resources of iron and other minerals, having those resources taken out of the ground in Canada and taken to the United States of America for manufacture. We cannot manufacture or process all of them in Canada. That is something which would be out of the question. But when we ship those exhaustible resources from our country we are in fact exporting employment and are denying to ourselves the development which Canada should achieve. These resources, processed to the maximum in Canada, will be the foundation upon which

development can take place, whereby population may be brought to Canada as by a magnet. I should like to see in this country not the kind of policy that would assure the maximum export of our materials in their raw state-which after all is, I think, a shortsighted policy; for when those resources are exhausted they cannot be replaced-but a policy that would assure that the maximum of development, fabrication and manufacture should be in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, in the first place I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) who has made his first non-partisan speech of the session. Better late than never. He cannot imagine now much his eloquence is appreciated when he speaks in the vein that he did just now. He quoted to us the Conservative platform about the national development of natural resources. He added "with the co-operation of the provinces".
The Conservative platform has changed a lot since the party met together for the election of its new leader, and the Conservative platforms at the present time are the utterances of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew). I did not receive a copy of yesterday's Hansard early enough to use it in these remarks, but I hold in my hand the Canadian Press report which appears in this morning's papers. I listened to the Leader of the Opposition yesterday when he read it, and I am glad to have it at hand. I shall read it again. The Leader of the Opposition's motion urged the government:
To consider a national policy under a system of free enterprise and in close association and collaboration with the provinces that will:
(a)	promote and develop all the country's natural resources for the benefit of the people of every part of Canada;
(b)	protect and conserve our forest, mineral and other resources from undue depletion or exhaustion;
(c)	expand the use of our resources for industrial production in Canada and thus create greater opportunities for the employment, advancement and security of all Canadians.
This is most interesting. I cannot understand the meaning of that proposal because it is supposed to act both ways. It advocates private initiative, and at the same time it is a purely socialistic proposal. How can the Leader of the Opposition advocate free enterprise, free initiative, and then suggest that Dttawa should make such commitments with regard to the natural resources of the country? The Leader of the Opposition was not in the house at the time, but I believe the hon. member for Lake Centre was-no, he was not, but he knows about it-when the 68108-302

dominion government transferred all the natural resources to the provinces. Ottawa no longer has any natural resources. There are national parks and things like that, but the soil of the provinces, with all its natural resources, belongs to the provinces themselves, and my hon. friends of the Conservative party should know that. Well, now, here they are. They want the dominion government, although they do not say so, to infringe upon provincial rights, and if not on provincial rights, on private initiative. They want statism, just as much as it may be practised in the province of Saskatchewan. I do not see any difference between the Leader of the Opposition and the premier of Saskatchewan; they are both advocating the same thing, and it is so much the case that yesterday-
The leader of the C.C.F. party does not agree with you.
He will agree with me.
Oh, no.

It is so much the case that
yesterday one member of the C.C.F. party, the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), realized to what extent the proposal of the Leader of the Opposition was illogical, and he suggested that the words "private initiative" be deleted, because the words "private initiative" are all lost in the proposal of the Leader of the Opposition. That is where my hon. friend the leader of the C.C.F. party will agree with me. Yesterday he voted for the subamendment of the hon. member for Kootenay West to delete the words "private initiative" from the amendment of the Leader of the Opposition. The hon. member for Kootenay West was perfectly logical, but I do not agree with his views because personally I am for private initiative. But I cannot be for private initiative and for socialism at the same time, as the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Lake Centre are.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
They voted the same way
last night.

Well, that is another illogical move, and it is quite disturbing. In their basket they offer socialism to the socialists; they offer the words "free initiative" to those who believe in free initiative; and they expect to get the votes of all by offering such contradictory proposals. Let them be more serious.
I have great admiration for the Leader of the Opposition. To my way of thinking he has done very well 'during this session, but he has spoiled it by his proposal of yesterday. There is no member of the house who

Natural Resources
has a higher regard for the hon. member for Lake Centre than I have, but why did he speak as he did today? Why did he support the amendment of his leader yesterday? I was stunned when I heard the Leader of the Opposition say that his amendment was seconded by the hon. member for Lake Centre. The hon. gentleman was not in his seat, and I was sure that the Leader of the Opposition was playing a little joke on him, and that when he returned he would explain that in his absence the Leader of the Opposition had thought that he would be ready to second the amendment but he had never heard of it, did not agree with him and that he was also the champion of free initiative. Instead of that, he spoke condemning the state policies jf the government of Saskatchewan.
No doubt we have had an advance copy of the speeches that he will make during the next election; but if I were one of the electors of the hon. gentleman I would ask him this question:	What is the difference
between your policy and the policy of the government of Saskatchewan? He could then tell the audience whether he is for socialism or for private initiative. Today we are all mixed up. He has blurred our vision and we do not know where he is leading us.
In the first place he must know that the natural resources of the prairie provinces as well as of all other provinces, with the exception of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon, belong to the provinces. He must know that. If he did not know it before, he knows it now because I am reminding him of it. Unfortunately the Leader of the Opposition is not here, so let the hon. member for Lake Centre tell him at lunch time that during the morning sitting he was told that the natural resources were returned to the provinces twenty odd years ago. I am sure that his leader will say to him, "thank you, John, for the information."
I am sure that the hon. member for Lake Centre will be only too glad to give that assistance to his leader and supply him with the correct information, because he himself wants to have ample information. He is never satisfied with the information given to him. But I have put this in a concise way, in a nutshell, so he can give the nut to his leader with the information in it.
We are coming to the end of the session and that is why the hon. gentleman has been exhuming and unearthing one of the planks of the program of the last convention that selected his respected leader. During the next election he will go to his constituents, wherever he chooses to run, and he will tell them:	We have wonderful natural

resources in this country and the dominion government is doing nothing to develop them. I made a non-partisan speech, the best of the session, and the Prime Minister said that they would do what they can with the cooperation of the provinces; but I am all for private initiative and I want, not the provinces-mark you-but the dominion government to develop our resources with the assistance of the provincial governments.
The hon. member started to rise a few moments ago when I said he was infringing upon the rights of the provinces. I know he will say that he is not. Whether the work is done by Ottawa or by the provinces, it is a kind of socialism and it cannot work. Private initiative belongs to the individual, the individual human being or the individual corporation, who is not run by or under the control of any government. That is private initiative.
I am sure we all know people who started at the bottom of the ladder without a penny in their pockets and made successes of their lives by being industrious and working hard. Finally they have become captains of industry and are now known as leading Canadians in the field of business. That is private initiative. Private initiative has done wonderful things for this country. I am strongly opposed to the kind of statism that my hon. friend is advocating.
We have great natural resources in the province of Quebec. The great Ungava ore fields are not being developed by the province. They are supervised to a certain extent by the province which has provided facilities to captains of industry who have decided to spend $300 million in order to build a railroad from the shore to the iron ore fields which are among the richest in the world. That was done by private initiative.
My hon. friend suggested the building of a road to the north in Saskatchewan. That would be very nice. To be built by whom? By the dominion government. In my county between Riviere du Loup and the border of New Brunswick is one of the finest highways in Canada. I went through the state of Maine last year and there was not a better road in that state than that section of highway No. 2 in my county. That was not built by Ottawa, it was built by the province.
If my hon. friend is suggesting that this road be built by Ottawa, is it not with the remote intention of telling his constituents at the next election that the men who work on the provincial roads are appointed by the provincial government, but if they will vote for him and they come to power he will name

all his supporters as road foremen on the dominion highway that is to be built from one section of the province to another? That is a way of cashing in on votes. If such is the case, I submit it is petty politics.
In my opinion it would have been better if the hon. member had told us that he was disagreeing for the first time with his leader who was sponsoring socialism and private initiative at the same time. He should have told us that he was leaving socialism to his leader while he would defend private initiative. Then I would have cheered him to the limit. I would have said that the hon. member was a man of conviction, was a man of principle, was a man who knew where he was going. I would say that he was a man with only one policy, that he was a logical man.
Instead of that he spoke to us about many things that were contradictory. He referred to the marshlands policy. These marshlands have been protected by repairing the dikes. That was advocated a long time ago by prominent Liberals like Mr. Veniot, the former premier of New Brunswick, and many others. That has been accomplished by this government. When we go to the bay of Fundy district in New Brunswick we see that the marshlands are in good condition because of the work that has been done by the Department of Public Works.
Then with regard to coal, the government gives the utmost assistance to the coal producers. With regard to hydroelectric power, why did the hon. member not mention Bill No. 109 which was passed this session to authorize grants in assistance to the provinces for the conservation of water resources? That was a most generous gesture on the part of the dominion government whereby 33 i per cent-
Thirty-seven and a half per cent.

-whereby 37i per cent of the cost is being made available for joint development work.
The hon. member spoke about trade. If he will look at page 4301 of Hansard of April 23 this session he will see that after his former leader, the Right Hon. Lord Bennett, had blasted our trade channels in 1935, the result was that when he left office our exports were $756,600,000; our imports were $522,400,000, making a total of $1,279 million. And in 1948, after thirteen years of Liberal administration, our exports were $3,075,384,000 and our imports were $2,636,945,000 making a total of $5,712,293,000- nearly five times more, after thirteen years.

If we export five times more, then do not other countries import five times more?
It is too bad the hon. member did not understand what I have said. I mentioned imports and exports.

But is it
not a fact that since 1935 all countries in the world have increased their imports and exports-in other words, increased their foreign trade-in about the same proportions as Canada?
And that is because in all countries of the world there were better governments than that of Lord Bennett.
Nonsense; ridiculous!

And in 1952, after the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) had been acting as such for four years only, Canadian exports were valued at $4,400 million and our imports were $4,050 million, indicating that, despite the tremendous figures involved, the difference between imports and exports was quite small. In other words the total trade in 1952 was valued at $8,450 million, and the difference between imports and exports in that year amounted to only $350 million.
I am astounded! I wish to congratulate the Minister of Trade and Commerce on the excellent work he has done since he has been in charge of that department. At this time I shall not repeat what I said on April 23 as reported at pages 4301 and 4302 of Hansard.
The hon. member for Lake Centre said that taxation should be at a lower level. Then he proceeds to suggest more expenditures. Does he have any idea of what his proposal will cost? No, none at all. He says, "We should do this" or "We should do that", in line with the obsolete Tory program adopted at the last convention of the Progressive Conservative party.
I will ask him this question: Can he submit some figures showing how much it will cost, now that the matter has 'been explained to him? Will he still advocate at one and the same time both private initiative and socialistic measures? And if he talks about tax reductions, what tax reductions does he advocate? That is another pertinent question. What does he want us to do away with? That is another interesting question.
Then he made reference to defence roads.

When does my hon. friend go to the Senate? That is one question I would ask.

I will tell my hon. friend that I do not know anything about it.
He has qualified himself for it today.

Probably I shall go there at
the same time as I go to the Supreme Court- since my hon. friend has been kind enough to give his recommendation for it.

I do not know how I could
do that; but I would be in the same position as he is when he states his policies. I would need the gift of ubiquity to be in different places at the same time-the Supreme Court and the Senate. My hon. friend is socialistic, and also for private enterprise:	I would be
at the Senate and the Supreme Court.

the Senate is socialistic?

I shall not continue with that discussion, because I wish to conclude my remarks as soon as possible.
The hon. member for Lake Centre has made some very poor arguments. He cannot answer anything I have said-or he tries to answer by making a little joke.
A red herring.

Yes, a red herring, a little
joke, by a most insignificant question. If he had something serious to say he would rise in protest and say, "The hon. member for Temiscouata is falsifying my statements, and I am anxious to correct him. I want the record to be clear." But instead of that he sits there and reads his newspaper, and he thinks of all I have said, and he looks sorry. Yes, he looks sorry because he did not realize earlier the mess in which he put himself and his leader yesterday.
What will the big subscribers to the Conservative party fund say when they read the speech made last night by the Leader of the Opposition? What will they say when they read the speech made just now by the hon. member for Lake Centre? They will say to them, "You have betrayed us. It is true that you spoke about private initiative but on the other hand you advocated socialistic measures. Our industries, our trade, will be taken over by the state if you ever attain power. We are afraid of you. We will not subscribe a cent to your fund because of what you and your leader have said."
Where are the old policies of the Conservative party in the days when it was not calling itself Progressive. Ah!-too bad!
I have only two further comments to make. The first is that I want this country to
IMr. Diefenbaker.]
prosper. Our natural resources are the great gift of the Almighty, and I agree that all Canadians should benefit directly or indirectly from them. But in virtue of our constitution and of the great differences in jurisdiction existing between federal and provincial rights in this country, each kind of undertaking should be done respectively either by Ottawa or by the provinces, or by private individuals who may enjoy the protection of all governments, including municipal and others.
We must respect our constitution. How many times have I heard leaders of the Conservative party speak about provincial rights? That is a good action-natural resources expanded through regular channels in virtue of the constitution, with the assistance that Ottawa may give to the provinces provided the provinces request it.
I see here my old friend and my dear friend the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Little) who practised private initiative to a rare degree by being a prospector in the north country. I salute him; I have high regard for him-and he is a typical example of private initiative in this country.
Hear, hear.

I can name many others who have done their share and who have taken a risk to do something that was different from what others did. They had the courage and the perseverance to make a success of their undertakings. My hon. friend, and others who are in the same class, deserve a particular tribute because they have shown outstanding qualities of good Canadian citizenship.
There is in this country a lack of certain categories of technicians and it is unfortunate that in virtue of the constitution it is impossible for Ottawa to intervene in matters of education. I cannot understand why there is not a propaganda campaign to have more engineers in this country. We need engineers very badly and we need geologists. We need men of technical experience who can help the dominion government, the provincial governments, private firms or individuals to develop this country. Not long ago I wrote to one of the cabinet ministers asking that some work of importance should be done at the earliest possible date. What was his answer? It was that we have not enough engineers. The Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham) told me that.
I am in correspondence with officials of the Department of Public Works and they too complain that there are not enough

engineers. We have too many bores who come along with degrees in social science and economics; but there are not enough who graduate in civil engineering. A practical suggestion is that although education belongs to the provinces in virtue of the constitution no member of parliament, including the hon. member for Lake Centre and the Leader of the Opposition, should miss an occasion to tell the people at large-and they have occasion to address large meetings-that we are in great need of engineers and geologists and men of real science. There is a fine future for them and not only will they prosper through graduating in such sciences but they will act as good Canadians and they will contribute to the progress of the country.
As a conclusion, I thank the hon. gentleman for what he said about the Prime Minister's meeting with the President of the United States. When he spoke there his remarks were apt and to the point. He said that in promoting trade with the United States, the government would have the support of all Canadians. That was very well said and it was highly appreciated when the hon. gentleman spoke that way.
The Prime Minister is a born diplomat and a man who is conciliatory. I am sure that his talks with the President of the United States will be of benefit to this country and that the hon. member for Lake Centre will have no regret whatever for having spoken as he did.
My final word, sir, is to say godspeed, a safe and happy return of the Prime Minister from his trip to Washington. I am sure that when he returns to Ottawa he will have good news to offer all. I also wish godspeed and safe return to all my colleagues from the journey they will undertake during the summer.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) always makes a very interesting speech. He usually states a case and then proves it to his own satisfaction even if it is not to the satisfaction of the rest of us in this house.
Thank you.

I want to join with him and with the hon. member for Lake Centre in saying to the Prime Minister that we wish him the very best of success in his journey to Washington. This is not a debate on trade and commerce, but since it has been mentioned may I say I believe that the future welfare of all the countries of the world, in every field, depends primarily on the
Natural Resources
policies of trade and commerce pursued by the United States.
Hear, hear.

If the United States continues to keep up barriers so that nations overseas cannot earn dollars that are necessary, then we are going to find ourselves and the other nations with us in very difficult circumstances.
Like others, I have been alarmed at some of the representations that have been made at Washington by American interests. I hope that when the Prime Minister goes there he will be quite explicit in what he has to say regarding the barriers that have been placed against trade and the violations of the agreements that have been made. I hope that he will come back with a report that will encourage all of us.
The hon. member for Temiscouata devoted a good deal of attention this morning to my friend from Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the allegation that the Conservative party at the present time is trying to ride two horses-the socialist horse and the free enterprise horse. The reason I rose before the hon. member was to say that I was going to vote against the amendment introduced by the Leader of the Opposition. The ground I was going to use and that I am going to use is that this resolution, this amendment, is restrictive. It says very clearly:
-that immediate consideration should be given to a national policy under a system of free enterprise and in close association and collaboration with the provinces that will:
And so on. In other words, my objection to this amendment is that it restricts the development of our resources to free enterprise and to free enterprise alone. What the other connotations of the amendment may be I do not know, but I know there is the explicit statement in this amendment that it will be under a system of free enterprise. My hon. friend implied, as others imply, that we in this party-because we believe in certain forms of social ownership, because we believe in the direction of social enterprise for the social good-believe that all enterprise should be run under some public organization or some state organization. That simply is not true, because I have always stated, and our movement has stated, that while we believe that the evolution is in the direction of greater social control and the development of our resources and of our instruments of protection, that development will be evolutionary and not revolutionary. It will come about when the people of the country decide that it shall come about, and not before.

Natural Resources
I remember very well a very prominent Conservative in this house-the member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) will remember as well-the late C. H. Cahan, when a matter of this sort was under discussion before, rising in his place and stating that very thing. He said that he did not know when the party of his hon. friend, who was then Mr. J. S. Woodsworth, would occupy the treasury benches, but he said he would have no fear when that day came because it would be the time when the Canadian people wanted such measures of socialization. They will decide that through the democratic processes, and it will not come about before. I should like to say this, too. While we hear a great deal of discussion about free enterprise, about socialization and so on, when I look across the way at the hon. members who are sitting with the hon. member for Temiscouata, I can say that I do not know of a government which, over a period of years, has done more to bring under social control quite a large number of enterprises.
During the speech by the hon. member for Lake Centre, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) interjected that the cobalt bomb was the result of public enterprise. I agree that that is so. The cobalt was sensitized in the Chalk River publicly-constructed, publicly-developed, publicly-owned and publicly-operated atomic reactor. The design for the so-called bomb was made in a cancer clinic in the city of Saskatoon, and was first used in the city of Saskatoon because it was designed there in a socially directed and free clinic for the treatment of cancer. The Minister of Trade and Commerce could tell us also of the very fine outcome of the manufacture of rubber, the Polymer plant at Sarnia. Again this is public enterprise.
When I look at my Conservative friends on my right, who have moved this motion trying to restrict all our efforts to so-called free enterprise, I would say that one of the greatest public enterprises on this continent, one of the most successful enterprises on this continent, is the great Ontario hydroelectric system. A Conservative government introduced that years and years ago. One might go on and point out that, step by step, we are approaching more and more a society in which, instead of selfish interests, selfish motives, giving the only impetus to economic and social development, we are having the social impetus and social conscience replace what is, after all, selfishness in the final analysis.
In saying that, I am not belittling what many people have done in the past in the realm of private enterprise and the exercise

of initiative. We do owe many of these people a great debt for what they have done in the promotion of the progress of the human race. But let me point out that very often it has been done at great social expense, great social suffering and so on. I want to say that, in common with every member of this house, I am sure we have great faith in Canada's future, great faith that if our resources are developed in the right way and in the right direction future generations of Canadians will benefit greatly from those resources which Providence has placed in this great land. Then, future generations will enjoy those resources to the extent that we conserve them now. When I say "conserve them", who is going to conserve them? More and more governments had to interfere because of the wasteful exploitation of the resources, in an attempt to conserve those resources for future generations. We have to direct, to some extent, the development of those resources. I prefer the word "develop" to exploitation.
I think that means an advisory council, but an advisory council that is rather more comprehensive than the one named in this amendment. I think the time has come when, in co-operation with the provinces, we should endeavour to set up a board that would assist in the planning of the use of these resources so that it would not be such a hit-or-miss idea as it is at the moment. If that were done we could both develop and conserve at the same time; that is the principle upon which our ideas are founded. We believe that there is a place for private enterprise in the development of our resources and the operation of our industry. We believe there is a place in national government policies, in the development of our resources by public enterprise, and that has been done as I have already indicated in the instance of the Polymer plant, the development of atomic energy and a number of other things that one could name.
There is a place for provincial ownership, provincial control and provincial operation of some of our resources. The first one that comes to mind is the production of power. Nearly all the provinces in Canada today are producing power under public enterprise. We find that is the best way. There are other activities which the provinces no doubt will find can best be done under public enterprise in the days to come. Then, there is municipal enterprise. In a good many instances the municipalities have undertaken quite wide services, and undertaken quite wide operations in the economic field. Then there is something that is not always looked upon as social ownership and social control, and

that is the co-operative enterprise. The people democratically get together in their organizations and decide that they are going to do something for themselves. Since I have been in this house I have seen a number of bills passed to make that sort of enterprise possible and to encourage that kind of enterprise, which is social enterprise. In many countries such as Norway, Sweden and the United Kingdom the co-operative organizations, particularly in the United Kingdom, are part of the Labour party or part of the socialist party in those countries. They believe that social ownership, through the co-operatives, is one means of promoting the cause of democratic socialism.
I wanted to say some of these things, and I admit quite readily to the hon. member for Temiscouata that the resources are in the hands of the provinces and that the resources must be developed under the control of the provinces. I think that there is nothing to prevent this parliament from assisting in every way possible the development of those resources in the provinces. I do not think there is anything that will prevent that action. I think that every encouragement should be given by this parliament and by the federal government to the provinces. The hon. gentleman says that the roads in northern Saskatchewan or northern Alberta are provincial responsibilities. That is true; and the provinces are putting roads into those remote areas as I myself know, because I have travelled over them. But what my hon. friend was saying was that if we are setting up all kinds of defence measures in the country and you have the Northwest Territories subject to attack as some think- although apparently Lord Montgomery does not share the view-or vulnerable and likely to be invaded in the event of war, then of course roads for military purposes instead of development purposes-although they might serve that purpose-are a matter for this house and for this government if they are part of a defence project. But if they are parts of a purely provincial highway system, it is a provincial matter and I would not argue in any other way. But I think that the government can make grants for the building of highways on certain considerations such as defence and national development of uranium and strategic materials.
I do not want to prolong this discussion, Mr. Speaker; it has already been rather long. I merely want to say that we hope the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) will be able to do something at Washington to open the channels of trade. I want to say that we are not voting for this amendment, because we
Natural Resources
believe that the amendment is restrictive; it restricts the development of our resources to a system of free enterprise whereas we believe that enterprise must be undertaken co-operatively. Let us have free enterprise, yes, where free enterprise can serve the public of this country; let us have free enterprise in that respect. Some things can be done by the dominion through this parliament. Some things can be done by the provinces. Some things must be done by the municipalities. We believe that much enterprise must be undertaken by the best form of social ownership through co-operative endeavour. Those are the points I wanted to make. As I say, as this amendment is a restrictive one, because it excludes everything but free enterprise, we are going to vote against it.
I was not here to hear the debate last night but when the hon. member was speaking I recalled that the way he was explaining the amendment was exactly the way that exactly the same amendment was explained by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) last year. As reported at page 3287 of Hansard of June 16, 1952, he said:
It was for that very reason that this motion sought to make it clear in advocating the further processing, as *Well as the conservation of these resources, we believe it is under the free enterprise system that this work will best be carried on and the highest measure of employment will be created.
That language was fairly explicit; and of course the amendment is even more explicit because it limits the development of our natural resources, the conservation of our forest, mineral and other resources and the expansion of industrial production-using the words of the amendment itself-to a system of free enterprise and none other.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say just a word about this motion moved by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew). Last night the discussion largely took place on whether the expansion and development for Canadians of our natural resources should be by private enterprise or by a socialist system. We Social Crediters are ardent advocates of private enterprise. We find that some people use the term "free enterprise" in much the same way as we use "private enterprise" and to mean the same thing. But opponents of freedom of enterprise have a different view of the term. They interpret free enterprise to mean licence, oppression, special privilege and many other ugly things which formerly were associated with the abuses of free enterprise rather than with a properly and fairly functioning free enterprise system.

Natural Resources
Last night we voted for the C.C.F. subamendment in order to make our position clear, namely that we do not advocate the kind of free enterprise that has associated with it special privilege, licence and oppression. With the C.C.F. amendment, the motion moved by the Leader of the Opposition is a perfectly acceptable one upon which we can put our own interpretation as to the method by which development and conservation of our resources shall be carried on. In his speech yesterday my leader made it clear that we Social Crediters favour resources development by private enterprise under intelligent government policy such as has been the pattern in the province of Alberta.
In respect of what?
In respect of the development and conservation of our natural resources.
Particularly our oil.

My friend the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) mentions particularly the development of oil; but as a policy I think that could apply to whatever development might take place in Alberta of our natural resources. We are prepared to support the Conservative amendment which includes the use of the term "free enterprise system" because we have made clear how we interpret that term. It seems that our interpretation is not much if at all different from that revealed by the Leader of the Opposition and the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in their speeches yesterday. Let me read without that phrase in it the amendment proposed by the Leader of the Opposition and let us see how it reads:
Whereas the natural resources of Canada are a heritage that should be developed and conserved for the purpose of providing the greatest possible measure of opportunity and security for all Canadians, this house is of the opinion that immediate consideration should be given to a national policy in close association and collaboration with the provinces that will:
And so on. Then follow paragraphs (a), (b) and (c), but I do not need to read them. To us, Mr. Speaker, that is a perfectly acceptable amendment and we voted for it last night. In reality, we see no reason why that should not have been a fairly acceptable motion for the entire house. We do not want to be accused of believing in socialism simply because we voted for an amendment which deleted the term "free enterprise".
You just want socialist votes.
We just want common sense ones; we do not want the others.
I did not think there were any earmarked votes in this country.

I may tell my hon. friend who has just interrupted so vigorously that we are not interested in socialist votes. As far as this party is concerned, and particularly we who come from Alberta, we do not expect any socialist votes, and as a matter of fact it would not make much difference because there are not many socialist votes out in our part of the country anyway.
There are only two left.
You will not get them.
With this explanation that I have made in respect to our belief in private enterprise it will be quite obvious that there is no inconsistency whatsoever in voting for both amendments.

No, we are not voting both ways.
Both sides of the fence.

My hon. friend now says we voted to strike it out. We did not vote merely to strike it out; we voted for the amendment without that being in. He now says that we are voting to have it put in. We are not voting to have it put in; we are voting for it with it in, and there is no inconsistency about that at all.
They know it.
And they know it.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. J. Browne (St. John's West):
speechtext: should like to make a few observations on this matter. I did not expect to speak on it and would not have spoken at all if it had not been for the observations made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) last night when he made reference to the developments that are taking place in Newfoundland. He said that he had been listening to a radio address by the premier of Newfoundland.
I said a press interview.

A press interview, and he was speaking over the radio. The hon. member is quoted at page 4763 of Hansard as having said:
A commission of government from Great Britain had to take over the administration of its affairs. Newfoundland is now part of Canada, but all during the time its development was unrestricted by government there was not very much development.
It is true, Mr. Speaker, that our development was not as great as that of Canada's;

but our country is not as large as Canada. If a comparison is made between the area of Canada and the area of Newfoundland I think that our development will be seen to be just as great as that of Canada's. The area of Newfoundland is only 40,000 square miles. The area of Canada runs into millions of square miles. Our population is only one-fortieth of that of Canada, and therefore I think the comparison is odious. But, sir, as a matter of fact, when you come to consider that we did not have the great resources that Canada possesses in her prairie provinces, and that we are situated in an area where the fisheries naturally had predominance, and when you consider the policy that was adopted by the government of Great Britain for centuries of preventing settlement in Newfoundland, then our slow growth is understandable. But apart from these features, Newfoundland did have some industrial development before the era of the present government there.
There was a time when Newfoundland was the greatest exporter of copper ore in the world. It is some time since that mine was exhausted at Betts Cove and Tilt Cove. Then we had the greatest iron ore mine on Bell island which is still in operation. Then, under the government of Sir Robert Bond, a paper plant was built back in 1904 at Grand Falls, and that today is a very profitable private enterprise that is still working.
At Corner Brook we have the largest paper mill in the world. It was started in 1925. Here I can give an illustration of the sort of collaboration and co-operation that exists between governments and private enterprise, because in order to get that plant on its feet the government of Great Britain and the government of Newfoundland each guaranteed $10 million worth of bonds. Neither one of them ever had to pay a cent under the undertaking. Nevertheless, the industry went ahead and is today very successfully operated under the management of Bowater's Limited of England.
The hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) has referred to the great Ungava iron ore development on the boundary between Quebec and Labrador. The huge sum of $300 million is being put up by private enterprise to build the railway, and that amount will be spent before one ton of ore will be brought to tidal water.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South said further:
I only heard a little of what Mr. Smallwood had to say, but he pointed out that his government did undertake the responsibility and developed three small industries, which they operated for a time. Later on they sold them.
Well, that is news to me. The three industries which he started were, one-

Everything is news to you, apparently, that is going on in Newfoundland.
I thought I knew something more than the hon. member.
You are not showing it.

Well, I think I do know a little more than the hon. member. When I asked a question whether they were paying he was not in a position to say. Nobody knows except the government because they will not publish any balance sheet, and they will give no information. If that is an example of what government enterprise can do, then I do not think it is worth emulation.
You will have to answer to Joey for that.

With reference to the three industries, one was the hardwoods plant situated about six or seven miles outside of St. John's. The amount of $1,600,000 was put up as capital, and $900,000 was supplied as working capital. The last report given by the manager, when the workingmen were looking for wages comparable to those in similar plants in Canada, was this: they were told to wait until the industry got out of the red before looking for higher wages. I have every desire to see that industry pay, because Newfoundland money is invested in it. Nevertheless it must be borne in mind that it was a very rash venture on the part of the government to go into a competitive industry of that kind without proper examination of what the conditions of the industry required and what the obstacles they had to overcome would be.
Another industry started on the west coast near Corner Brook was a cement plant built by Latvians with German machinery, which has broken down several times since it was started, and which has recently been sold to the German firm that built the machinery plant at Octagon at the formal opening of which the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) was present. That company has paid for it with what? With a note, and not a cent has been transferred, according to the information received.
That is private enterprise.

Breton South (Mr. Gillis) had made about the transfer to private control of certain industries in Newfoundland which had been started by the government. I am very glad to see that take place. I hope they are going to be successful. I think the premier of Newfoundland has found from experience that the running of industrial enterprises by the government is not as simple as he thought, neither is it as simple as some members of the C.C.F. party have tried to persuade us that it is.
There are certain enterprises of a monopolistic nature, such as telephones, railroads, telegraphs, the supply of water and sewage facilities and so on in municipal areas, which are ideally suited for public ownership, but it seems to me that ordinary industries confined to the production of a single article are not generally suitable for operation by a government. I think it is a good thing that the premier of Newfoundland has decided to sell these to private industry.
I think it is only fair to give him credit for the best of intentions. As I heard him express his position, when we came into confederation he realized suddenly that unless there were some large enterprises in Newfoundland people would migrate to the mainland or go to the United States. It was with that in mind that he decided to use the large surplus of $50 million, which was quite a large sum for a small country like Newfoundland to have saved, and put a certain amount of it into the construction of these three projects, the hardwood plant, the cement plant and the gypsum plant. I did not know that the gypsum plant had also been sold to private enterprise.
The next part of his program was quite different and I think much sounder. In that part he decided to advance fifty per cent of the capital required to establish certain industries. He induced German industrialists to come to Newfoundland to establish several industries in that way. I hope that they will be successful also. However, I feel sure that the general principle of the government operating private industrial ventures is an unsound one and this was not originally realized very fully by the premier and government of Newfoundland.
Third, the government of Newfoundland set up a government-controlled corporation, the Newfoundland-Labrador development company, and passed over to them a large section of Newfoundland and Labrador for the development of natural resources contained therein. Since then the premier has made what I think is a better move by inducing a private group of industrialists

headed by the famous Rothschild banking house of London to come and establish a new corporation, which is popularly called BRINCO, which is short, I think, for British Investment Company.
This year and for several years to come they will conduct an examination of a large tract of territory, containing I think about 20,000 square miles. At the end of each five years a certain amount of that territory is to be passed back to the government. I think the premier of Newfoundland as he gets more experience is showing better judgment in the sort of venture in which he is investing Newfoundland capital or to which he is assigning Newfoundland resources.
It seems to me rather difficult to reconcile some of the statements made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South with those made by the leader of the C.C.F. party. I could not see very much difference between what the Leader of the Opposition or the Prime Minister said and some of what has been said by the members of the Social Credit party, and what the leader of the C.C.F. said. He did not seem to be so much against private enterprise.
However, he did speak of co-operation, and I think it is generally understood by all that there has to be co-operation by the federal government, the provincial governments and industry. That goes without saying. That has been done everywhere. It has always been done, but owing to the two great wars and the extent to which government intervention in industry was necessary, the part played by governments in industry has been much greater than it otherwise would have been if private enterprise had been allowed to keep on going.
As the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) has said, it is the duty of the government to take a supervisory attitude toward industry and to see that the people who are working in industry are properly looked after. That is why we have laws regulating labour and the other conditions which attach to the workingman in an effort to bring about a better distribution of wealth.
I think we are all agreed that we would like to see as much co-operation as possible in the country, co-operation among the working people, co-operation between industry and labour, co-operation between governments, so that we get the best possible balance between them all. I do not think it is possible for a government to run all the affairs of a country without having communism. I do not think it is possible for a government to run most of the affairs of a country without having conditions which would be akin to those in

communist countries. As I say, there has to be a balance.
It seems to me that I remember one of the leaders of the C.C.F. party in British Columbia saying something which was much stronger than what the leader of the C.C.F. said in this house today. It may be only an echo in my mind, but I think I remember reading that a leader of the C.C.F. party in British Columbia had said that if they had socialism they were going to have it with the army and all that goes with it. It seems to me that that was going very far and certainly it is not desirable.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South made one or two other statements to which I should like to refer. Referring to the credit that should be given to the premier of Newfoundland, the hon. member said, as reported on page 4763 of Hansard of May 4:
It was the initiative, drive and courage of the Newfoundland government that actually got something done. Nothing had been done under the system of free enterprise.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South is a very experienced speaker and I enjoy listening to him. I find that as a rule he has a most sensible approach to the problems of this country. However, I am sure that what he said yesterday was not really what he meant to say. He could not have meant to say that at all. He was carried away by his feeling against private enterprise and his enthusiasm for socialism. He then went on to say:
Whether or not we agree with what the gentleman did, in my estimation he has done more for that part of the country since he formed the government than was done by all the free enterprisers without government interference.
Now, there is an extravagant statement.
Rescued from bankruptcy.

That is not in line with the usual common-sense statements attributed to the hon. member for Cape Breton South, particularly when we come to consider that the fishing industry in Newfoundland is one of the greatest examples of private enterprise, and that for over 400 years it has been carried on at all points around the coast of Newfoundland, where the fishermen have their little homes and have their own capital invested in vessels, boats, traps, nets and other kinds of fishing gear. Each man is a little capitalist on his own.
Always starving to death.

No, not
always starving to death. Conditions were bad at times, as they have been in other industries.

Nothing to eat but turrs and murres.

I do not
think it becomes my hon. friend to interject an observation of that kind; because I am sure he must realize that when he makes a statement like that I cannot allow it to pass without making some comment about it. I know something about the part of the country from which my hon. friend comes. Many Newfoundlanders have gone there to work in the mines. I have only one other comment to make. The hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot)-I do not know why-during the course of his speech this morning made reference to the increase in trade between 1935 and 1951, and showed that it had increased many times over. I asked him if, in view of the fact that the exports of Canad-a had increased fivefold, the imports had not been five times as large, too. That is all it amounts to. Imports and exports balance each other. If we export five times as much, than someone else buys five times as much. We are then in a position to import five times as much.
There has been a rapid development of trade in the intervening years between the depression days of 1935 and the present time. During that time the value of money has depreciated. According to the figures of the dominion bureau of statistics, the cost of living has gone up to the extent of nearly 90 per cent. Freight rates have increased by 98 per cent. So that the value of all commodities today, in 1935 money value, is very different. That has an important bearing on the question at issue.
Trade naturally has increased because the population has increased. I do not think the hon. member for Temiscouata really appreciated what he was saying, or that he

I was also surprised to know that hon. members of the Social Credit party in the House of Commons agree with the attorney general in British Columbia who, in a letter sent to the board of transport commissioners, indicated that he took no interest and was not concerned in transporting oil by way of the United States for refineries there, rather than in Canada.
