Mr. Speaker, the amendment before us is an interesting one. It is unfortunate however that it could not be discussed without raising the subject of provincial politics. As a matter of fact this happens to be the type of debate that should be possible without having the subject of politics enter at all. Unfortunately, however, so long as we have our party system of government I suppose that is impossible.
The amendment calls for a new national policy. The phrase, coming as it does from the leader of the Progressive Conservative party, has an historic ring. Some hon. members have questioned why the leader of the Progressive Conservative party should introduce a debate at this time on a national policy. To me the reason is quite obvious, though I would be the last person in the house who would want to impute motives to the leader of the Conservative party.
I am sure you will pardon me if I admit that I surmise there is a very close connection between the two sets of facts that confront us-first the introduction of a debate on a new national policy and, second, the fact that we are approaching a federal election. Apart altogether from that, I think

every party in this house agrees that a national policy for the development and conservation of our natural resources, such as is envisaged in the amendment, would be a good thing for Canada. I can quite understand why the Progressive Conservative leader would introduce a debate of that kind at this time. I can also understand why the Prime Minister just cannot accept that amendment. As he indicated, it would be an admission on his part that the government today is not following any such policy.
Of course, those of us on this side of the nouse are inclined to agree that while the government has in the past years taken many forward steps in the development and conservation of our natural resources, nevertheless there has been no general well-planned policy for that purpose. In our opinion, of course, the government has been far too much concerned with the achievement of the objectives set forth in the Conservative amendment to have had much success in that respect. The government has over the years been far too much concerned with the preservation of so-called free enterprise to have succeeded very fast or very far with the development or the conservation of our natural resources.
The amendment is interesting in that it calls for a national policy to develop and conserve our natural resources for all Canadians and, at the same time, it calls for the preservation of the free enterprise system. Apparently one is just as important as the other to the party which introduced this amendment. I presume that the preservation of the free enterprise system and the conservation and development of our natural resources for all the Canadian people are more or less synonymous with the Conservatives. I presume they consider them to mean one and the same thing. That has been Conservative thinking over the years and it would now seem that the leader of the Conservative party wants us to adopt a national policy tied to the free enterprise system which he hopes may achieve for Canada what the earlier national policy adopted by a Conservative statesman did for Canada in past years.
I think I should point out that we have had two periods in our history when Canadian governments and Canadian political leaders have caught the vision of a national policy and the great development of Canada's resources. The first was during the time of the Conservative leader Sir John A. Macdonald, and the other was carried out by a great Liberal statesman, Sir Wilfrid Laurier. One sought to build Canadian industries and the other sought to open up for us the great resources of western Canada. I think we
Natural Resources
should also bear in mind that neither of those policies was carried through strictly as a private enterprise policy. In the building up of Canadian industry under the first Conservative national policy the government had to come to the assistance of private enterprise in the form of tariff regulations. The government had to impose tariffs against importations in order to protect those Canadian industries. It was not by any means a development carried out by private enterprise unassisted by the government. Nor was the opening up of the western prairies a private or free enterprise project. Primarily the government of Canada took the initiative, gave leadership and provided the means whereby the prairie provinces were opened to development. I submit that if we attempt to enter upon a period of great development of our natural resources, under a policy tied to the free enterprise -or capitalist system, we are simply trying to turn back the hands of the clock at least fifty years. I would say that the present Progressive Conservative leader, in attempting to tie his national policy to a free enterprise system, is more conservative than was the great Conservative leader Sir John A. Macdonald in the early days of our history.
Today industry has become revolutionized. Today we have entered upon an era of mass production and there is today no such free enterprise as was known in this country fifty years ago. If you doubt my statement and you have a few dollars, try installing a gasoline pump and undertaking to sell gasoline to motorists-as a private or free enterprise. You will find out about the kind of competition that you will come up against. Fifty years ago, yes, a man with $2 could probably do that. Today conditions have changed and today competition in big business at least is between giants and the small free enterpriser gets squeezed out of existence in the process of trying to compete.
Try developing the resources of this country under a system tied, as this amendment visualizes, to the free enterprise system- and that, I submit, is putting back the hands of the clock. This amendment is more reactionary than I thought the leader of the Conservative party could possibly be at this time.
The opposition of the Social Creditors toward this amendment is a little more confusing, to say the least. They support the amendment with the provision that it be done with free enterprise included, and they support the subamendment to delete the words "free enterprise". They explain to us that what they mean'by "free enterprise" is a sort of free enterprise known only to Social Crediters, a converted free enterprise, a free

Natural Resources
enterprise system that has been changed apparently under the direction and influence of Social Credit. I must admit that I do not know just what that free enterprise system is, that so-called Social Credit free enterprise. There again, while I would not want to impute motives, it seems quite obvious to me that Social Crediters are trying to appeal, on the one hand, to those who consider themselves capitalists, and on the other hand to the mass of the people who have votes and who are not any longer wedded to capitalism.
The situation in the world today indicates that the so-called free enterprise system, which has prevailed for the last one hundred years throughout the world, has pretty well outlived its usefulness. Let it be granted that in the process of that evolution the free enterprise system served its purpose just as did the other economic systems before they were followed by the free enterprise system. But if we take a look at Africa and Asia, where European countries guided by the free enterprise system have been in control for one hundred years, we find that we have a revolt in Africa and Asia against the kind of free enterprise which those countries have imposed upon those people.
Today, in my opinion, the free world in its approach to those countries and those peoples is making the mistake of confusing free enterprise with democracy. Some of the countries that are showing an interest in raising the standard of living in those countries are just as much concerned with the maintenance of free enterprise within their own countries as they are in raising the standard of living of those people. Today, I think we must recognize that we are in a period of evolution which comes very close to being revolution. Today the world is undergoing a process whereby the free enterprise system is giving way more and more to socialism. Whether we like that or whether we do not, we find the world will be moving more gradually towards the adoption of democratic socialism. If we are to save the world from communism, it will never be saved by the free enterprise system. It will be saved only when those who desire to save this world from communism are prepared to accept democratic socialism and develop the resources of this country and all other countries, not primarily for the profit of those who invest capital but primarily for the benefit of the people who live in those countries.
We hear a great deal about the essential need of capital. The member for St. John's West (Mr. Browne) has told us what invested capital has meant to the development of

Newfoundland. I could tell him some things to show what invested capital has meant in the development of Newfoundland. I think I could dismiss that subject by telling the member for St. John's West that he and his party opposed the most progressive step that was ever taken by Newfoundland, and that was confederation. If their support of the free enterprise system in Newfoundland or anywhere else is in line with the reactionary point of view they took in connection with that matter, then I think we can pretty well dismiss it. We must lift our sights. We need a new national policy. We need a policy directed by a government which is not wedded so closely to the free enterprise system that it could lose sight of the needs of the people.
What has the free enterprise system done for the natural resources of this country over the years? Go to a place like Rainy River and look at the dump of sawdust and slabs that represents a once prosperous community. This dump was left there by private enterprise after it had despoiled the forest resources of the country and then moved out, leaving the people who had worked for that company for years to go back on municipal relief. Think for a moment of what has happened to the timber resources of this country. What is happening to our minerals? What has happened to other natural resources? It is true that men have found employment, but are men not entitled to employment in this country? You can develop natural resources without private enterprise capital, but you cannot develop natural resources without the brains and brawn of human beings. Let us not forget that. It is much easier for governments, if they are so inclined, to find capital and put that capital to work in the interests of developing our natural resources, but more essential than capital are the brains and brawn of the people who work in that field. If you are going to adopt a national policy, then let us not lose sight of the fact that the people who are to benefit first and foremost through that policy must be the men and women of the country and not the capitalists who invest their capital. Let us not confuse the preservation of the free enterprise system with the development and conservation of our natural resources.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say just a word or two before we take the vote. The statements concerning trade made by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold-well), in my judgment, put the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and those who are going to visit United States officials into an extremely difficult position. Those statements are just like the ones the government-bench members use but they are completely unrealistic. I hope that before long we in Canada can get the idea that we do not have to sell in the United States as many goods as we think we do in order to be able to survive as an economy. In order to give our people some idea of the position the United States is in, I feel it is only fitting that I should read a report by the Associated Press on page 8 of the Ottawa Morning Citizen of yesterday.
Washington-Six cabinet officials will testify this week on a single issue packed with political, economic and international implications-tariffs and trade.
The House of Representatives ways and means committee announced Sunday that State Secretary John Foster Dulles and Treasury Secretary George Humphrey will lead off today in a parade of administration witnesses on a bill to extend the reciprocal trade act for one year.
The secretaries of commerce, agriculture, interior and labour, and mutual security administrator Harold Stassen are to give their views Tuesday and Wednesday.
Such a line-up of top officials on a single bill was taken in some circles as indicating the Eisenhower administration will fight a move led by some powerful Republicans in congress to bolster tariff walls against some foreign goods.
Politically, the bill could have important repercussions. The chief sponsor of the bill is Representative Richard Simpson (Rep. Pa), chairman of the congressional campaign committee-the group that will work with Eisenhower to try to hold and strengthen Republican control of the house in the 1954 elections.
Economically, more than two score witnesses told the committee last week, the issue means life or death to scores of American industries allegedly threatened with destruction by growing imports of cheaper foreign goods.
Internationally, relations with free world allies will be affected. Britain, France, Germany, Japan and other nations have argued eagerly that they need to sell more products to the U.S. here to bolster their short supply of dollars.
I ask hon. members this question: When a nation is in the throes of difficulties like that, can we with any appearance of grace at all approach that nation with accusations that

Natural Resources
she is breaking her faith in respect of the international agreement on tariffs and trade and that kind of thing, which we have heard, in my opinion, all too many times in this house from altogether too many men. Surely the United States has the right to govern herself as she sees fit without a lot of whining and badgering from Canada. If we are unable to deal with our international trade situation, let us see if we cannot find a solution with the British commonwealth. We would not have any trouble doing that.
She will not buy our wheat.

I agree with the hon. member that we would not be able to sell our wheat unless we used the device which Canada's finance minister used in world war I. If the hon. member will take the report of the royal commission on banking and currency in Canada, published in 1933, and will read that report with an open mind, he will be able to see how we can sell our wheat abroad by simply using our national credit. It was done back then. Surely it can be done now by the same device. We have the testimony of Sir Thomas White, who was the finance minister responsible for the eight years in Canada during which the great monetary experiment was made to the effect that the whole operation was not inflationary but was sound.
Let us just stop talking nonsense about selling our goods abroad. There is a way out. That is enough for me to say in that respect.
I wish to say that the Social Crediters are not going to take the position in respect of United States trade that the hon. member for Lake Centre and the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar took. There is a ray of hope in trade without hurting anybody. Let us remember that the United States is rapidly approaching a condition of being self-sufficient. She is being aided toward this objective by great machines and improvements of technological skills and additional uses of solar energy. Anyone who is realistic at all will make allowances for the phenomenal influences of these three factors. It is true the United States could buy zinc and some other raw materials which we cannot afford to sell too much of, but I cannot see any means whatsoever whereby the United States in the interests of her own economic security could possibly accommodate us to the extent that we want to be accommodated, and feel we cannot live if we are not so accommodated.
I should like to spend just a minute or two on some of the extravagant things that have been said by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank)-who I think made a real spectacle of himself this afternoon in

the face of the facts-and by some of our C.C.F. friends. We Social Crediters will grant that we are fighting the British Columbia election. We will grant that the Social Credit party is going to do everything in its mortal power to put the C.C.F. out of business in British Columbia, and the C.C.F. are going to try to do the same to Social Credit. But we do not need to say foolish things; we do not need to distort the truth. Let us get the facts just as they are, and on the basis of those facts fight the election. Let us not say exciting and inflammatory things. Social Credit does not intend to do that. If the C.C.F. cannot fight their election without using that kind of method it indicates weakness in their position; that is all. I have nothing to say against the C.C.F. except to say we believe they are all wrong; but we want to get the facts of the situation.
The good member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) has been greatly disturbed about the position the Social Crediters take on enterprise. The finest possible example you can find of the action of private enterprise that Social Credit believes in is the oil industry in Alberta right at the present moment, where an absolutely phenomenal development has taken place; and it has taken place as a result of very wise governmental management of private enterprise. If Alberta had allowed enterprises to be absolutely free, if we had allowed the oil companies to be completely free in Alberta, two or three of them-
Will the hon. member-
Let me put my case, and then you put yours. Then you will get what I have to say and you will not be foolish.
He does not want to hear.

He does not want the people to hear the truth. If we had permitted the big concerns like the Imperial Oil, Standard Oil and others to go into Alberta, if we had permitted them to be completely free, two or three of them would have acquired possession of the whole oil industry in Alberta, and they would have been at liberty to develop it or to refuse to develop it in accordance with their own wishes. The Social Credit government made up a set of rules which completely restricted them in respect of monopoly. It was impossible to get a monopoly because of the method we adopted. The government set up a method under which these companies had the least possible chance to lose money as they went hunting Alberta's oil, and the greatest possible chance of having success, of finding and developing oil. All these facts are easily

acquired by anyone, even by the hon. member for York South, if he wants to get the facts. If he does not want to get the facts, well, nobody on earth can get him to get the facts.
But the system, as I said a moment ago, in connection with the Alberta oil industry, is an ideal example of what Social Crediters mean by individual enterprise, not free enterprise going in to destroy the value of the resources, or to monopolize them or to mismanage them in any way, shape or form Nevertheless, with government assistance in the way of providing knowledge concerning the various fields in Alberta, and then the other things, private enterprise was able to do a magnificent job in Alberta. In 1948, if I remember correctly-and I am speaking from memory now-we had sixty companies of all sizes and strengths drilling for oil in Alberta all at once, and the weakest of them completely certain of measures that would protect them against infringement by their big neighbours, and the big fellows completely certain that they were not going to be discriminated against.
I think I have said enough. I wish the hon. member for Fraser Valley were here because I had a word to say to him. I do not intend to say anything against him while he is away. Those few points needed to be clarified just a little. May I say this once more to everybody concerned, Liberals, Conservatives, C.C.F.'ers and all the rest of us. In fighting the British Columbia campaign let us play the game clean and square. Social Crediters are going to do that; and if you do not, shame on you.

We have been getting a lot of good advice yesterday and today, some of it scientific, some of it liberal and some of it practical, on how the job of the development of our natural resources should be carried on. I think we have heard enough. Let the government get on with the job, supported by the opposition.
I was paired with the hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Gagnon). Had I voted I would have voted against the amendment.

maintopic: PROPOSAL TO ESTABLISH LIVESTOCK MARKETING BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to raise a grievance. No consideration has been given to the setting up of a livestock board. I have raised this problem before but I have never been able to get very far with it.

The farm organizations have always asked for a board with producer representation on it. The function of the board would be to administer, under the Department of Agriculture, the Livestock and Livestock Products Act, and the members of the board should be appointed in consultation with organized agriculture.
The Livestock and Livestock Products Act should be amended and consolidated with other legislation in order to place in the board the power to license, regulate and control the facilities for assembling, transporting, yarding, slaughtering, processing and packing, together- with the facilities for grading and selling of all livestock and carcass products designed for human consumption. The board would need also the power to make such levies on the products under its jurisdiction as would be necessary to defray the costs of its operations.
The position with respect to the United States market today is that, while the embargo has been lifted, there is practically no trade at today's prices. It seems more necessary than ever that we should have a board to supervise the marketing of our livestock. It may be necessary for us to have further cold storage facilities to carry the heavy supply over from one season to another. On previous occasions when I have raised this matter in the house, many different arguments have been made against it. One was that the farmers did not want any more control, and on another occasion the minister said it would be difficult to find the money. He thought, too, that there might be some doubts as to the legality of a measure such as this.
Since 1867 there have been great changes, and no doubt it may be necessary to introduce an amendment to the British North America Act because the production of livestock has increased to such an extent since that time. Today there is a pronounced trend towards larger business organizations. In many cases the small businesses have disappeared altogether or have been absorbed by the larger concerns. The meat packing industry as well as other distributing organizations have in general followed this trend, and a larger part of the purchases of western livestock is represented today by the purchases of three or four packing concerns. The concentration of buying in the hands of the relatively few firms creates a condition of imperfect competition, because markets may be unduly affected by the buying operations of one or all of these large buyers.
About thirty years ago the farmer had a lot to say in the selling of his livestock. I can recall that the dealers would be out meeting the farmers to bid for the livestock

they had in their sleigh or wagon. In many cases we drove the cattle into town. Later the trucking of livestock became popular and everything went to the stockyards of the abattoirs by truck. The hogs were left at the packer's, and the packer sent a cheque. If you were dissatisfied you had no appeal, and you still have no appeal. You accepted what you got, and that is the position today. The farmer has lost all his bargaining rights so that it has become more necessary than ever to have this livestock board.
The farmer could have his cattle rail-graded, but the same conditions do not apply as in the case of hogs. The grades are set for hogs, but in so far as beef is concerned you just have the two grades, red and blue. Everyone knows that there are many other grades in connection with cattle. The increased trucking to the packing plants instead of to the public markets'has resulted in the loss of the services of experienced commission salesmen who knew the market from day to day. The elimination of the central, competitive market would probably put the producer at a considerable disadvantage in selling to two or three large buyers. If we are to establish fair economic returns and security for the primary producer, I do not believe we can ever again rely upon the automatic processes of what in the thirties was erroneously termed the "free competitive market."
I always recall what Donald Gordon said in one of his speeches. He said:
Selfish and private interests must be ruled out completely and the competitive system must be replaced with one which is based entirely upon the criterion of maximum production.
Even if that statement was made during the war, it is still true today in so far as the Canadian livestock producer is concerned. The boards which have been set up by the government for different purposes have demonstrated beyond doubt that they can develop a steady market for a product and remove price fluctuations. Fluctuating prices have always been detrimental to the farmer. Prices change not only from season to season but from day to day, and this is detrimental to the farmer.
The production of livestock is a very important branch of agriculture. If the fertility of our soil is to be maintained, something will have to be put back into the soil. It is an established fact that the best way to maintain soil fertility is to raise animals on the farm. I think it is an established fact also that the best way to market some of our crops is to feed them to livestock, and then market the livestock. Ttue commission on price spreads in 1935 dealt with stockyards and public markets. I think one sentence in that
, 1953	4799
Proposed Livestock Marketing Board report deals with what I have been saying. I quote:
When many competing sellers are faced by few buyers who act in concert, or who tacitly agree to follow the lead of larger buyers, exploitation becomes possible.
This statement is just as true today as when the commission wrote that report. I am happy to have this opportunity of bringing this serious problem of the livestock producers before parliament. I hope the government will give serious consideration to the following:
1.	The establishment of a national livestock marketing board upon which the producers from each province will be adequately represented, to be charged with the responsibility of setting and maintaining a fair and adequate floor price for livestock, with fair price spreads for different grades.
2.	The provision of the necessary additional cold storage and processing facilities in western Canada. These are to be made available to the livestock industry on much the same basis as the government terminal elevators are made available for grain, that is as part of a national program for orderly handling and processing much needed foodstuffs in the long-term interests of both the producers and the consumers.
3.	In so far as sale policy is concerned, the products are to be divided into two classes, namely that portion required for consumption in Canada-this being by far the majority of livestock products-and the portion for exports. The board should establish a price based upon a proper and fair relationship to other goods and services within our own Canadian economy. Secondly, the balance of the products over and above our own Canadian requirements should be handled exclusively by the national livestock marketing board and be disposed of in world markets to the best advantage of the producer on a straight sale basis, if possible, or if necessary by a barter arrangement.
In closing, may I say that I hope the government will give consideration to this request so the livestock producer may have some security and stability in the marketing of his livestock.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just wish to say a few words in support of the setting up of a national livestock marketing board with producer representation thereon. We in this group have, for a number of years, supported what we call a two-price system, namely a system under which agricultural products in Canada will be sold at a price that bears a fair relationship to the price of other commodities, and our surplus agricultural products should be exported
4800	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Proposed Livestock Marketing Board abroad and sold for the best price that can be obtained, preferably through some form of international food agreement similar to the international wheat agreement.
I think there is no question that if a two-price system were to be introduced, the most efficient way by which it could be carried out would be through the establishment of a national livestock marketing board similar to the wheat board. The wheat board has received strong support from the farmers in western Canada. I remember that, before it was set up, many people questioned whether a compulsory board of that kind should be set up; but since it has been in operation it has received the overwhelming support of the farmers of western Canada. I am satisfied that a national livestock marketing board, under good management, could give similar satisfaction.
I realize that if a board of that kind is to be set up, a plebiscite should be taken in the provinces, and that it should be put into operation only provided that a substantial majority of the farmers-we will say a two-thirds majority-supported it. Then of course enabling legislation on the part of the provinces would be required in order to make operative a national marketing board of that kind.
I know there are many people who oppose boards of this kind. They say it is not fair to compel the farmer to deliver his produce to such a board. But I have always noticed that most of the people who raise that point are themselves not farmers at all. They are so lacking in consideration for the welfare of the farmer that they do not want him to have a board of that kind upon which there will be producer representation. But generally speaking we find that the farmers themselves, and the farm organizations, are strongly in support of such a board.
Those people who oppose boards of that kind say there is only one way for farm products to be sold, and that is under the law of supply and demand. In my opinion the law of supply and demand is a joke, and a very bad one at that. The law of supply and demand takes into consideration only the demand represented by the people who have the money with which to buy. It absolutely ignores the great needs of a large percentage of people who have not the money with which to buy; it therefore does not take those people into consideration at all. Consequently, when the farmers expand their production to the point where they could satisfy the needs of the starving millions in the world, in view of the fact that we have no method by which those goods can be made available to those people who have not the money with which to buy them, the goods become surplus and

prices fall. As a result, under the so-called system of the law of supply and demand farmers are discouraged from expanding their production because they know that if they expand their production the prices of agricultural products will fall.
Speaking at the annual convention in Victoria, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) recognized that fact. He recognized the fact that by expanding our production of livestock and creating a surplus-not a surplus in so far as the actual needs of the people of the world are concerned, but a surplus in so far as we have an actual paying market for them-we would be faced with this difficulty. He therefore recommended to the farmers at that convention that they should reduce their production of livestock.
I am not criticizing him for doing that. He was doing it with a realization of the present situation, and a realization that if they expand their production with such a situation existing, prices will be forced down and farmers may well get less for their increased production than they were getting for their smaller production.
On the other hand, if you had a livestock marketing board operating on the two-price system, the farmers would at least be guaranteed in the home market a price that bears a fair relation to the prices of other commodities. That price might be on a basis similar to that under the Agricultural Prices Support Act, or it might be on a basis similar to that in the United States, namely 90 per cent of parity which is based upon the years 1909 to 1914.
When we consider the fact that there are in the world today, according to the food and agriculture organization, millions of people on the verge of starvation, no great producing country has the moral right to tolerate a situation where farmers are encouraged to reduce their production. I believe that a national marketing board is a sound way by which there can be built up a policy which will encourage farmers to produce at the maximum level, with the guarantee of fair prices for their products.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words in support of what in other circumstances would have been a resolution by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce), had there been the opportunity to move a further resolution.
I think what occurred when the foot-and-mouth disease broke out in Canada should be an object lesson to the government, to indicate that there is some need for regulation. When the foot-and-mouth disease broke out we found that there was confusion between the provinces and the dominion as

to where jurisdiction lay. Agriculture comes jointly under the jurisdiction of both the provinces and the dominion. Until in the livestock industry we have some board set up making regulations and working out a system of co-operation between the dominion and the provinces, we are always going to find ourselves in the position we are in today.
Agriculture finds itself in this position, especially the livestock producers. Small surpluses may completely upset the market. Our home market can and does absorb by far the greatest portion of our production, but a small surplus of 10 or 15 per cent in meat products, in beef or in pork, may completely upset our market because either the government must take it off the market, as they have done to a certain extent now under the Agricultural Prices Support Act, or it must be sold in the markets overseas; and the 10 or 15 per cent that goes into the overseas market sets the price for the whole domestic market here in Canada. That is the consideration which alarms our agricultural producers. They do not want that to happen. It has happened in the past and no doubt it will happen again.
There is need for certain investigation into the spread between what the consumer pays for livestock products and what the producer receives. Last fall, I believe it was on October 7, an order in council was passed here in Ottawa supporting the prices of certain low grades of beef; I refer to canners, cutters, and so on; the three or four lowest grades. Under that order in council the government purchased beef from the packers at from 33 to 37 cents a pound; I believe it was 33J cents in Saskatchewan and 37 cents in Ontario and Quebec. Under that order in council I believe they purchased over $5,600,000 worth of those low grades of beef. During the time they were purchasing that beef of those particular low grades, the live animals were being sold by producers on the market at from 6 to 8 cents a pound. Yet the government were purchasing this beef from the packing plants at from 33 to 37 cents a pound. Of course, when the packing plants were selling beef to the consumers of this country they based their prices on the prices the government were buying at, not on the prices they were paying the farmers for that beef. The result was, as I see it at least, that it did good neither to the consumer nor to the producer, but it did give a guarantee to the packer.
We should have a board of livestock commissioners to regulate and to get co-operation between the provinces and the dominion in the regulating and selling of our meat products. The Canadian Federation of Agri-

One of the reasons it is very difficult to operate such a board was demonstrated just a few minutes ago by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright). When the government gets into business or activities of that kind it is most difficult to have a discussion on the question at all without having matters misrepresented.
Last year we were buying beef and pork because of foot-and-mouth disease. We had to do it whether we liked it or not. Now I am told that cattle were selling at 6 and 8 cents a pound at a time when I presume the hon. gentleman intended us to believe that beef from the same cattle was bought by the government from the packers for 37 and 38 cents a pound. The hon. gentleman knows, or at least he ought to know because he has been told many times, that the government did not buy any meat last year with the exception of meat that came off animals that were purchased at the price which bore the proper relationship to the floor price of

Proposed Livestock Marketing Board live cattle. The floor price of live cattle was set, and when any packer attempted to sell beef to the government he had to be able to demonstrate that that beef came off animals for which farmers had received at least the floor price. There was not any time at which that price would have been related to the prices that were stated here a few moments ago.
But the chief reason it would be difficult to have a board of the kind that has been described in connection with meat is the great difference that exists between the marketing of cattle and hogs and the way in which they are processed after they are marketed, as compared with what happens to wheat. I noticed that the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) kept pretty much away from any suggestion that the board should be like the wheat board; but the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) repeated several times that it was largely because of the great success that has been achieved in the marketing of wheat through the wheat board that he suggests the same thing might be done in connection with livestock.
The wheat board is set up with its headquarters at Winnipeg, and practically all of the grain that is marketed through the wheat board passes through Winnipeg. A very small percentage of it does not, but nearly all of it does, and any person can have his grades checked. After the wheat reaches the market anywhere west of Winnipeg, where the grain has been taken in by the producer, if he is not satisfied with his grade he can allow the wheat to go on down to Winnipeg and have it rechecked there before or after the car arrives there. Thus there is complete control over the situation all the time, and the farmer is able to have his product completely checked two or three times before it actually gets to the market, if he wishes. That does not happen in connection with the marketing of livestock.
I suppose there are tens of thousands of butcher shops and packing houses all over the country, and most of the cattle that are taken in are slaughtered at some point or other a long distance away from where there could be any control whatsoever. It is impossible to have someone out to control the grades at all the points, just as it would be with grain if you had small mills everywhere. But the supervision of the controls is all at one point. There is no one point at which you could supervise the control of livestock grades; and since there is not, you cannot carry it out in the same way it is carried out in connection with the marketing of wheat under the wheat board.

There is of course the possibility of doing something about it by having more than one board, by having a number of boards. If one were to handle it in that way, as suggested by the hon. member for Selkirk, it would require to be a provincial set-up, and you might require ten boards if you wanted to handle it right across Canada. There is a possibility of doing that, but a board established here to do that would run into so many difficulties and so much trouble that it would be almost impossible to operate.
I know I will be asked what I was asked last night and did not reply to, because the answer is obvious. If it is legal to do it in connection with wheat, why can it not be done in connection with livestock? The obvious answer is that one is a product which everyone knows ought to be handled in the way in which wheat is handled. It is a product only about 20 per cent of which is consumed in this country, and a large percentage of it is not consumed where it is grown. It is consumed at a distance away, and the wheat all has to pass through Winnipeg. Therefore everybody agrees what is the practical way of doing it. But there are not 10 per cent of the livestock producers in this country who will agree that you could do that with cattle and hogs.
No one has ever tested whether it is intra vires to do the thing we are doing in connection with wheat. No one has taken a chance on testing it. It has been discussed in this house scores of times since I came here as to whether the method we are following in marketing wheat is constitutionally sound. Nobody has ever undertaken to take it to the courts to find out.

People go to a meeting and some fellow gets up and moves something and often there is never anything said either for or against before they pass it. The hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), who I think was at the meeting, made a remark a few minutes ago with regard to what I had said in Victoria. I did not say what he said I had said. A man got up and said I had said that, but I proved to his satisfaction right after that I had not.
My hon. friend said I advised them at that meeting that they ought to keep down their production in order to get higher prices. That is not what happened at all. It is all down in black and white because I read it, so there is no reason for not being able to show what I said. I told them that we had had conferences here every December attended by representatives of all the farm organizations, and the provincial and federal governments. Those representatives sat down and discussed the whole situation. As a result of having discussed it, the farmers went home and decided not to produce so much of this thing and to produce more of something else. They themselves determined what they were going to do without being

I repeat that when the government gets into many of these things, or even gets talking about them, there are a lot of people who do not understand them nearly as well as they do when they are doing business with somebody else. I am not at all surprised at the stand taken by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). It has taken the grain producers of Canada 50 years of fighting, year in and year out, to get the degree of stability in grain marketing that we have today. Fifty years ago grain marketing in Canada was just as haphazard as is the marketing of livestock today. The speculative market was open; dockage was excessive; farmers did not in those days have the right to order a box car to deliver their grain. They were at the mercy of the elevator companies.
The position of the grain producers 50 years ago was exactly the position of the livestock


producers today. In connection with livestock today there is no stability and there are no regulations. Prices fluctuate day in and day out, year after year. The minister says the livestock producers in Canada would not favour a livestock marketing board. I am sure they would. They want a livestock marketing board, and for the precise reason that in the last 18 months livestock prices have fallen by 40 per cent.

Today in the livestock industry a few of the major packing companies are buying the vast percentage of livestock that goes on the market. And if the minister says that with tens of thousands of butcher shops they cannot be controlled, then in effect what he is saying is that Canadians are not law-abiding citizens. And I do not believe that suggestion at all. I believe if regulations were laid down, and if a law were brought in setting forth the various grade standards and various prices to be paid for livestock, that in nine hundred and ninety-nine cases out of a thousand those prices and regulations would be followed in every respect.
We in this group do not believe we are going to have that kind of stability in the livestock industry at an early date. It will be a long, hard pull, a long, hard fight. But some day we will have in connection with the marketing of livestock products a measure of stability in the same way as we now have it in wheat marketing.
Yes, the minister can raise one problem after another. There are problems; but we do not think those problems are insurmountable. We feel that it is an injustice to the livestock producers to have a condition wherein they must accept, as they now must, prices that fluctuate to such an extent as we have seen in connection with beef, where the price fell by 40 per cent in a period of 18 months.
The minister says, "Well, we never were successful in closing the grain exchange." That was a standard excuse for a long time, that the grain exchange was under provincial
Supply-External Affairs jurisdiction. We do not need formally to close the Winnipeg grain exchange in order to have it closed in a practical sense. All we have to do is to make sure that all the grain being sold is handled through the marketing board, and that none of it is allowed to go on the grain exchange. The board will be operating, and the exchange will not be dealing in grain futures.
I would like the government to bring in a measure which would provide stabilized marketing for livestock products. If it did that, and asked for the co-operation and support of farm organizations it would receive that support one hundred per cent. If it were to ask for the co-operation and support of provincial governments, before long that support too would be forthcoming. Mr. Chairman, I believe it is customary when the first item is called to make a brief statement concerning the work of the department. I assure hon. members that mine will be brief, because I made a fairly exhaustive review of the international situation when I last spoke in the house, and I feel there is not much I can add at this time to the review I then made.
However there are one or two observations I should make before we begin the consideration of the estimates themselves. First I should like to pay my tribute to the work of the standing committee on external affairs, whose report is before us. The report, as hon. members know, shows that the committee, after careful and conscientious consideration, approves the main estimates of this department. It does make certain recommendations to the government. Some of these recommendations are in connection with general international matters which are not exclusively within the competence of this government; but our policy in regard to them does, I think, fall in line with the recommendations. There are some special recommendations dealing with a number of problems within the competence of this government.

Supply-External Affairs and it is recommended that those matters should be kept under review. I have no hesitation in saying, Mr. Chairman, that those recommendations are useful and constructive, and it will be the policy of the government to do its best to give effect to them.
I would just like to say a word now, Mr. Chairman, about the United Nations general assembly session which has just recessed, and also a word about the North Atlantic council meeting which concluded in Paris about a week ago.
So far as the United Nations general assembly is concerned, it completed a very long and arduous session about ten days ago, the latter part of which I confess was conducted in a friendlier atmosphere than that to which we have become accustomed at United Nations general assembly meetings. The assembly is not adjourned, it has merely recessed; and by resolution of the assembly the president is instructed to call it together if the talks now going on at Panmunjom should lead to an armistice, or on a request of a majority of the members. Whether or not the talks will result in an armistice is still a matter for speculation. The United States negotiators there are showing the patience and perseverance which they have shown in the past, and if there is good will and any reasonable desire on the part of the communists for an armistice it should be possible to achieve one. I say this because the latest proposal of the Chinese communists and the North Korean government which was submitted to the president of the general assembly on the question of prisoners of war does to a very considerable degree bridge the gulf which previously existed between the two sides on that vital issue.
It is too early to say whether those talks will result in an armistice, but I would hope that they will not be broken off by those who are negotiating on behalf of the United Nations without consultation in advance with all the governments which have forces operating in Korea. I feel sure that this will not be done, and I would certainly hope that it will not be done.
It is of interest to note that, if an armistice should be signed, and I underline the word "if", one section of the present draft agreement provides for the calling of a political conference. If we get an armistice and if the fighting comes to an end in Korea-and we must all hope for that-then we will be faced with the problem of a political conference dealing with questions concerning Korea and, indeed, possibly covering other Far Eastern questions related to Korea. The relationship of the United Nations to that conference will be something that must be

worked out, and it will not be an easy problem. The United Nations general assembly itself, consisting of 60 member governments, might not be the best mechanism for working out a political settlement in Korea in the first instance.
That, Mr. Chairman, is all that I think I have to say at this time about the United Nations. There is a good deal more that I could say, and I have no doubt that questions concerning the United Nations' activities may come up in the course of consideration of the estimates. If so I will, of course, do my best to deal with them.
Before I sit down I think I should say a word or two about the North Atlantic council meeting which ended in Paris a week ago last Saturday and which was attended by my colleagues the ministers of finance and national defence as well as myself. It was a useful and I think a constructive meeting- although it was not spectacular and was not meant to be so. One of the reasons we finished our work in such a short time was that the permanent council is now meeting regularly in Paris, and all the preparatory work had been done before we arrived there.
It was not only a useful meeting; it was a very timely meeting, because it occurred at a time when all the governments of all the peoples represented were intensely interested in the meaning of the recent Soviet moves and gestures which seemed to many to presage an easing of tension, and therefore might mean a move toward peace. We had indeed an interesting exchange of views on that subject.
I might mention the results of the work of the council under the following headings. First we discussed the annual review procedure by which we take stock of our defence preparations and plan for the future. In that stocktaking much emphasis was laid on the relationship between economics and defence. That emphasis was recognized by all delegations and especially, if you like, by the delegation from the United States, as being very important at this time. At Paris we agreed on both firm short-term defence programs and longer-term provisional plans.
In the communique which we issued at the end of the meeting, and which no doubt hon. members have read, it will be noticed that we merely spoke about decisions which had been taken and which it was hoped would result in a notable increase in our defence strength over the Lisbon figures for the year 1953. No figures were given in the matter. We departed from the precedent of Lisbon where a figure of 50 divisions in appropriate stages of combat'readiness was mentioned, and about

which we had some interesting discussions at the last session. This time we merely talked about a "notable increase."
The omission of figures was deliberate and was agreed upon unanimously. It was felt that as we were getting stronger and building up our forces and defensive strength there was no real purpose to be served by officially communicating figures of that growing strength to those who would like very much to have them and who are not particularly friendly to us. It is one thing to have those figures appear in the press as a speculation or as someone's guess, intelligent or otherwise, but it is quite another thing to have those figures officially confirmed by the NATO organization. Therefore we did not do so.
There was another reason why numbers were omitted. It was that we felt that concentration on quantity in a defensive buildup tended to take our minds off qualitative build-up. At this North Atlantic council meeting a great deal of emphasis was placed on increasing the quality of our defence forces as well as increasing their quantity.
As it is five o'clock, Mr. Chairman, if it is agreeable I shall resume after the conclusion of private members' hour.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as one who had the privilege of serving on the standing committee on external affairs this year and of taking some humble part in its discussions, before I launch on any general comment with respect to our present external position I should like to have a word to say in connection with the deliberations of the committee and its report.
While the committee did approve the estimates, there were some things in them that caused the raising of some eyebrows among committee members, and I think perhaps properly so. One must recognize the fact that when the word "approved" is used by a committee such as that, it means approval by the majority of the committee, of course. Although in this case we did not try to make any division within the committee itself, having in mind our attempts always to keep our foreign affairs policy as free as possible of political divisions, one of the things that we in the opposition have always concerned ourselves with in following a multiple-party policy in connection with foreign affairs is the fact that some of the details of the methods of handling foreign affairs, if great vigilance is not exercised, could perhaps become almost uncriticized estimates or uncriticized policy, something which would not be good for parliament, for the government or for the people.
One or two matters particularly came up for consideration in these discussions which I think perhaps ought to be mentioned. One is the question of the cost of embassies which are proposed to be built in certain countries. One of those embassies which caused the most difficulty in the committee, so far as criticism was concerned, was an embassy that it was proposed should be built at a cost of something like three-quarters of a million dollars. I think the committee's discussions had a fruitful result with respect to that matter, because I am satisfied that the department will stop, look and listen with respect to that expenditure. Although it may be argued that the money comes from blocked currency in that particular country, nevertheless it is actually Canadian money that is being expended; and I think it is necessary that we should watch carefully expenditures on that kind of work.

Supply-External Affairs
The other matter I wanted to raise is the question of the C.B.C. international service. I do not intend to elaborate upon the matter at this time, but it caused some concern to the members of the committee who reached the point of having the director, Mr. Jean Desy, brought before the committee to give evidence. Of course the international service is or should be in close liaison with our external affairs policy, largely because of the fact that Canadian foreign policy is embodied in every broadcast that is beamed to other countries. One of the things that has concerned me most is that, even after the evidence was given by Mr. Desy in the committee, it seemed to me that still closer liaison ought to be brought about because the policies he pursues in Montreal are not under the Secretary of State for External Affairs but under the Minister of National Revenue with whom he works.
That divorce between the two departments might conceivably lead to some difficulties later on that we ought to try to avoid. One of the problems is, what are we beaming to other countries? It is only fair to say that we were given some samples of what is being beamed to these countries behind the iron curtain and elsewhere. But it is pretty difficult for a committtee to have anything more than a peep through the window as to what is going on, and we had that peep. I do think there ought to be very close and continuing supervision by the Department of External Affairs with respect to each one of those broadcasts.
For instance, I think it was a bit of a shook to the committee to learn of one broadcast that had been arranged to Brazil. I have nothing against a good musical broadcast being made to Brazil, but it does seem to me that when we get into such astronomical figures for a broadcast for an hour, or however long it was, of the order of $24,000 odd- perhaps it can be justified-it should not be repeated, shall I say, without some careful and close scrutiny and attention being given to it, because it is so easy to overstep the mark, in connection with some of these expenditures. It is only fair that I bring this to the attention of the committee today as one of the things that did concern us in connection with the committee's hearings.
In addition there was the age-old problem of the issuance of passports, with which the minister is thoroughly familiar and which came up again in the committee. Some of the members of the committee, including myself, have been concerned with the issuance of passports to people who go roaming around behind the iron curtain to no good purpose so far as the Canadian people
fMr. Graydon.I
are concerned. I know there are a lot of difficulties in connection with that, and the minister has pointed them out to me, and so has the department. But it does seem to me that we might have gone a step further in our recommendation, although I know certain members of the committee did not want to go any further at this time. We could have gone further and called for some kind of conference between the two departments of citizenship and immigration and external affairs for the purpose of seeing to it that our red-tinged Canadian citizens, or so-called Canadian citizens, who go behind the iron curtain with such impunity have some sort of bridle put on them to prevent them from disgracing this country over there or when they come back here at will.
These are things that occurred to me as being rather important that came out of the committee itself.
Added to that was the matter of the St. Lawrence seaway. I am one who would have liked to see the committee go further in the report with respect to the St. Lawrence seaway, because it seems to me we ought to make ourselves pretty clear in this country with respect to the attitude of the United States congress to that question. I have been wondering whether we have not been perhaps a little hesitant about taking the gloves off with the United States congress in respect to this matter. I noticed that the Minister of Trade and Commerce did go a considerable distance in New York not very long ago in connection with that particular point, but I do feel very keenly that the United States congress ought to be told very plainly by this parliament that its delay and hold-up in connection with the completion of the St. Lawrence seaway are not looked upon with favour by the majority of the Canadian people.
In addition, it seems to me that in connection with that matter we have not been told by the government at all times just what delays can be expected in a legal and constitutional way. I have been greatly concerned about that. On a number of occasions I have asked the Minister of Transport some questions; I asked General McNaughton some questions when he was before the committee, and I am not at all satisfied yet that we have come to the end of all the legal delays and red tape that the United States congress and others in the United States can put in the way of the completion of this great project, which is of such importance to the people, particularly in my part of the province of Ontario, and of Canada. We ought to be told very clearly exactly what we might expect in that connection, because sometimes we

have glossed over the difficulties and the obstacles that are likely to arise in the hope that the rising sun of the great St. Lawrence seaway, which has so far been delayed, may soon be seen. These delays have not come about by reason of anything Canada has done, but by things that have been done unnecessarily and improperly by the congress of the United States and by some of those who have been lobbying for their own purposes in connection with other means of transportation in that very important part of the international boundary.
Then the question of the charter revision was a matter for the report. It was a matter that I raised in the house, as the minister knows, in the early part of the session, before the committee was set up. I am glad the committee decided to do that, because I would like to see Canada in the very forefront of the amendment to the charter of the United Nations. We cannot start too soon. The next session of the house ought to see the standing committee on external affairs dealing with that, because it is going to take more than one session. It may take two sessions, and by that time 1955 will have rolled around and the revision of the charter will come up for decision in the general assembly.
We had a great part in setting up this charter at San Francisco, and certain provisions of the San Francisco charter contain more words put there by Canadian representatives than were put there by the representatives of any other single country. We can be proud of that, and I should like to see that developed and carried forward into the next revision, because Canada cannot afford to be behind. We have always been in front, and I should like to see us stay there.
These are some of the matters I thought I might deal with in a very brief way with respect to the committee's report. When the minister makes his reply, or during some period of the discussion, I should like him to deal with another matter which was not raised in the committee itself, and which should have been. It has to do with the military attaches who are attached to some of the embassies all over the world which are manned and operated by Canadians. These also include the embassies we Rave in NATO countries. That would seem to me to be unnecessary because, in addition to that, we have military attaches at the seat of the NATO organization itself.

I suppose one of the most important things that has happened since the last time we met and discussed foreign affairs in any broad way is the death of the premier of Russia and the advent of the new administration, or whatever one likes to call it over there. That of course has caused great changes in the thinking and speculation throughout the world, as to whether or not it means an approach to peace or is only the old policy done up in a new package.
I was quite interested in one comment made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South not so long ago, not on a debate on external affairs. When the hon. member talks common sense I always listen to him, and I think this was common sense. Just at the moment I cannot think of many times when he has not talked common sense, but we will not go into that. One thing he said I think was like him, because not many people in the house have had perhaps as close association in trying to fight the reds in Canada as has the hon. member for Cape Breton South. I give him full marks for that. One of the things he said was that the moves of the government in Russia were more a change in tactics than a change in policy.
That being the case I think it is only natural that the people on this side of the iron curtain would look that gift horse, if you want to call it a gift horse, in the mouth. We have had a lot of experience with the Soviet union in the past and to expect that they are likely to turn into angelic forms overnight is perhaps testing the credulity and common sense of the people a little too much.
As the minister says, I think one ought to test everything that is being done. If these people are in earnest, if they are genuine and if this offers a road to peace, then we want to go along that road with them. I think that is what the Canadian people want. But on the other hand we must watch that we are not being faced with a situation such as we used to describe down on the farm as follows: Do not let them buy us at one end of the market and sell us at the other. That is the one thing that bothers me in connection with the whole Russian approach.
It is much easier for a dictatorship to change its policy overnight than it would be for this government or the government of the

Supply-External Affairs United States, of Great Britain or of any NATO country which would have to carry along a great democratic body of opinion with them. You cannot take a curve and change overnight when you have a load of public opinion behind you. They can turn and twist as they like and as they did in 1939, just before the war broke out, after berating the Germans for years. We all have memories of the cooing doves of the Kremlin towards Hitler which would almost turn the stomach of anyone who was interested at that time in seeing that international justice was being done.
I am concerned about whether this change is genuine. I believe we know enough to watch. I think the policy that we could very well follow would be one of care, courtesy and common sense. It would be too bad if we found that we had been the victim of some diabolical plan intended to bring down our guard and weaken our defences so they could turn upon us when we were weak.
That is what we have to watch for. I am stating this in Warn and direct language, perhaps not in very diplomatic terms, but I think they indicate pretty well what the average Canadian is thinking. I think we have to be pretty careful, and I believe the government realize that because they have not let down in their NATO obligations or plans. I am not so sure that we are not seeing the fruits of the NATO plan being realized now. I am not so sure that the fact that there has been a leading through strength in our diplomatic channels for some years has not had a great deal to do with the strengthening of our position and the change of mind and heart, if it is a change of heart, in Moscow. I have always said and I still maintain that up to the present time they have understood only the language of force and strength and might. Unfortunately, whether we liked it or not, we had to speak that language in order to make them understand. Now that we are speaking that language perhaps they are understanding to some extent just what we mean, and that we mean business in our international affairs in connection with peace.
I should like to make one other observation in connection with our general United Nations policy. Some years ago I made a statement in the house, and the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) put it in a different form during this session. I subscribe heartily to what he said. I am not criticizing Canada in this regard because I do not think Canada can be criticized, but I think a lot of other countries are open to criticism in that in the past even some of the big powers have made a plaything of the United Nations general assembly.

To my knowledge there has never been a general assembly meeting at which the heads of all the states were present at the same time. It is one thing to say that the cornerstone of the foreign policy of a nation is the United Nations, but it is another thing to do something about it. We have sent two prime ministers to the United Nations general assembly, but there are a number of heads of states who have never been at the general assembly in any capacity. Those countries send their permanent representatives to Washington or New York, their second-string men, if you want to call them that.
It seems to me that if the United Nations is going to succeed there must be some reasonable approach made by the heads of states and an attempt made to attend. One of the troubles we have with the people behind the iron curtain and on this side of the iron curtain is that the heads of states never meet at all. The place for them to meet is not at a special meeting; they should sit down at the United Nations general assembly and tu' their feet under the :ommon table in an effort to thresh things out and try to arrive at some peaceful settlement of the world's problems.
Surely that is not asking too much of the heads of states if they really believe that the United Nations is the powerful instrument it was intended to be, that is for the protection, preservation and maintenance of peace and security throughout the world. I do not think it is too late for that sort of thing to be carried out as it should be.
I should like to mention one other matter. When we were dealing with the matter of foreign affairs previously a great deal of anxiety was expressed by many hon. members of the house over the new Eisenhower program, particularly as it related to the Far East. Well, I never felt that way and I so expressed myself in public.
A number of people expressed concern about it, and you would almost think that the peace of the world was being shaken by what President Eisenhower had said about the neutralization of the strait of Formosa. Whether it is because of what he said, strangely enough instead of having been a threat to peace the world seems to be moving toward lessened tension. More than that, I think most people realize now that to have criticized that policy was going pretty far. I felt that the new United States policy held at least a fair chance of success. I do not think anyone is apt to make the same statement he made two or three months ago, particularly when he realizes what significance attaches to the Eisenhower policy put forward only two or three weeks ago, when the United States indicated what they were

prepared to do in the interests of disarmament and world peace. I think that proposal of the United States government was about as sane and sensible as anyone could expect from any democratic nation in the world.
The thing that struck me most forcibly and I suppose struck the humanitarian heart of everybody was when President Eisenhower said that, after all, if we could only disarm progressively and properly throughout the world, we would have that much more money to spend upon the needy and underprivileged and underdeveloped all over the world. I think they deserve credit for having put forward such a sane and sensible policy, and I hope that will not be subject to unnecessary criticism as time goes on.
One thing does seem indicated, as we change from one era to the other, in the matter of soviet diplomacy. Up to the present time we have been faced with aggression on the military side of the picture; and that aggression on the military side has caused us no end of trouble and no end of concern. It has been a kind of cold war aggression; but it has always been there. There has been extensive pressure, when no one on this side of the iron curtain seemed to be quite happy or satisfied that we were not likely to run into trouble almost any day.
That has not been a very healthful climate for our people, or indeed for the peoples in any part of the world. Today, perhaps because our military preparations, through NATO and in other ways, have become more developed, we are now moving into a new era; and it looks to me as though we may be faced now with aggression in the field of world trade.
That is a concern shared, I believe, by all hon. members in parliament. We recall that it was not long ago, shortly before the death of the Russian premier, that a question was raised from the Kremlin indicating that there was a move afoot to divide the free nations. And in the light of bilateral agreements made by Russia which have been disclosed from time to time, I do not mind telling hon. members I am greatly concerned that even right now we may be in an era when the soviets are content to soft-pedal military aggression, and in the alternative are whooping up aggression on the international trade front.
If that is so, then I think this government, in company with the governments of other free countries, had better watch its step. Because it seems to me that in the days that lie ahead our prosperity, and all those things for which we stand, could easily be endangered if in some fashion or another our trade were undermined by this new policy of soviet 68108-304J
Supply-External Affairs aggression. If they lay emphasis on that phase of their activities, then we must meet the challenge. It seems to me that whatever is required, all free countries-and particularly the United States, which has a big stake in the matter-had better watch very carefully the position they take. Because today, when trade is so greatly sought after, and at a time when the soviets may be angling for all kinds of bilateral agreements with people who need trade, they may dig deeply into the trade position of many of the free nations.
While I have not given up the idea of the urgency of our military requirements, and the priority that must be given to them, it would seem, if one may judge from reports, that the urgency of military priority might be a little less than it was before. I do suggest it has reached the point where we can back up. It would seem that we have met some of the urgent necessities connected with that military problem. I believe, however, that we have now reached a time when, without in any way sacrificing our military position, it is essential, in our position in-NATO, that we pay some attention to article 2 of NATO to which the minister referred a moment ago. I know there are some difficulties in connection with freeing the channels of trade. Nevertheless, when they have to, people find ways of doing things. However, they are not prone to follow that course if they do not have to, or if they do not want to.
It does seem to me that if in NATO we are going to meet both the military and economic aggression, we must see to it that a careful review is made of our channels of trade, as applied to all countries in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, to see to it that, having met military aggression up to a point, we shall not neglect the aggression on the other front and leave our back door wide open so as to invite trouble from that quarter.
I realize that my remarks have been rambling because, rather than prepare a speech, I have spoken extemporaneously. I do hope, however, that when we meet again to discuss foreign policy in this great chamber of parliament, we may be immeasurably closer in a genuine and honest way to those days when sunshine and peace will shine permanently throughout the world. Because, after all, I suppose there is no single thing about which members of this parliament dream and for which they long more than the days when the threat of war, with all it implies, shall have been removed from the face of the globe, and people are allowed to live in decency, peace, harmony and Christianity.
