Mr. Chairman, when the debate on external affairs took place two months ago I was not able to be in my seat. Consequently I should like to participate in this debate and make some observations regarding the general situation that I think has changed since the earlier debate took place.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs said he had made a statement at that time, and that perhaps what he said then would, in a sense, suffice for the general statement that might otherwise have been given. It seems to me, however, that in the immediate past there have been some quite phenomenal changes in the international picture. Undoubtedly there has been an immense change in Russian statements-whatever the deeds may be-since Marshal Stalin's death a comparatively short time ago. And of course it is fashionable to say

we all say it- that what we should look for are deeds, not words, as evidence of good faith on the part of the Russians in the peace gestures they have been making.
But I think it is well to remember that in a propaganda battle, in the cold war, words sometimes, in themselves, become deeds. Russian propaganda both at home and abroad has been sharply changed lately. Soviet newspapers, for example, are suddenly discovering the importance of personal freedom lor Soviet citizens. That is something new. The whole Soviet system of extorted confessions has been dramatically exposed. Suspicions many of us entertained about inexplicable confessions have been confirmed .by the Soviet union itself.
Then there has been an entirely new attitude displayed in foreign affairs. The west, for example, is no longer the butt of column after column of vicious, hysterical attacks in the Russian papers, particularly in Pravda and Izvestya. This sudden change in Russian propaganda would be significant itself; but followed by some of the events which have actually taken place, let us hope that it really is indicative of some change in Russian policy. Nothing comparable has occurred throughout the whole of the Stalin era; not even the purge trials of the thirties were accompanied by such changes in what appears to be Russian policy.
I should like to look at just a few of these changes, as a background for what I am saying. First of all they have been instrumental in releasing British civilians in North Korea, civilians who had been imprisoned since the outbreak of hostilities in the summer of 1950. Then they granted amnesty to two million prisoners in the Soviet union; at

least we are told they have. Of course we have no proof of it; but that is what they say. One of the most extraordinary announcements of all, I think, is that they have acquitted the nine Jewish doctors who had been condemned and sentenced for alleged misdeeds against certain prominent members of the soviet ruling class-indeed, conspiracy to murder those leading citizens. What seems to me to be more extraordinary is that they have subsequently proceeded to punish those who had used the power of the police state in securing the conviction of the accused doctors, and it is admitted that the confessions had actually been extorted by what they themselves called vile means; and they have condemned the use of such methods.
They have indicated a willingness to exchange sick and wounded prisoners of war in Korea as a prelude to truce talks; and, as we all know, an exchange of sick and wounded prisoners has since been carried out. The communists have indicated a willingness to resume the peace talks in Korea that were disrupted last October. Those peace talks, whatever comes out of them, have at least been revived and are now in progress.
I think we can take note of this, too. In the middle of a very tense situation which had arisen over the shooting down of allied planes by the Russians in the Berlin air corridor, the Russians came forward with specific proposals for a system of air travel to Berlin which might help avoid these incidents in the future. Those are all gains. Then, too, we have the fact that an informer, a woman previously lauded to the skies for what was afterwards admitted to be a piece of patriotic perjury, is deprived of the Order of Lenin. Not so long ago a- soviet captain was punished for allowing the sailors of his ship to go ashore and fraternize with the residents of the country they visited. However, three weeks ago soviet sailors were permitted to visit Paris and, indeed, even to express the view that it was an agreeable city at least to look at. For the first time in years a group of United States newspapermen, paying their own way of course, were given an opportunity to visit Moscow and move about freely, it is said, and even to take some pictures.
Then, of course, we have something which concerns us in the United Nations, in the matter of the appointment of the new secretary general of the United Nations. That broke a deadlock which had existed for several years.
What does all this mean? Any one of these incidents might not in themselves appear to be significant, but taken together they

surely must be regarded as indicating a hopeful change in the Russian attitude or the attitude of the new administration in regard to Russian policy. All of us hope- I see that an hon. member shakes his head. I did not say it was a change in policy; I said let us hope that it is a change in policy.
I do not agree.
Surely the hon. member can agree with that hope.
I can agree with the hope.

That is all right. I say all of us sincerely hope that these adjustments may at least pave the way for ending the cold war and building a secure peace. That is what we have to hope, even if at the moment-and no doubt this is in the minds of members when I am saying this-we have to maintain our defences and let none of them down. Let us hope and welcome any move which will seem to indicate a change of attitude and change in policy, or the opportunity to end the cold war.
Now all of us are guessing; there are lots of guesses as to the reasons for these developments. Perhaps some people think they result from a struggle for power in the Soviet union. Perhaps they are felt necessary by the new Russian administration to strengthen their hold upon the Russian people. Perhaps they are indicative of a different political outlook by the new Russian leaders. So far we can only speculate on the reasons for the changes.
I think one thing we should bear in mind is that it would be quite unrealistic for us to expect a complete reversal of the whole Russian position in the world. Such expectations and hopes might lead us to make prerequisite demands on the soviet leaders which, from their point of view, would be extremely difficult if not impossible to meet. I think we have to keep in mind that it would be foolish for us to expect, for example, that the new soviet leadership could convert Russia or her satellites into democracies overnight. I wish we could hope for that, but it would be unrealistic to hope for such a thing.
It would be equally foolish of us to expect, as President Eisenhower appeared to do in his speech of April 16, that the Russians will suddenly agree to free their satellites and withdraw beyond the Oder-Neisse line. Certainly they will not do that until after a long period of pressure and negotiation. To base our policy on such expectations and demands, is quite unrealistic. Indeed to make some demands, such as President Eisenhower did, as conditions prerequisite for the reopening
Supply-External Affairs of negotiations with the communists on outstanding issues, is to place unnecessary obstacles in the way of peaceful settlement.
The present situation provides us with certain magnificent opportunities which I do not think should be lost. There has been far too much emphasis on caution since these gestures were made, too much of what might be termed "go slow, watch and see". There is a place for caution, and I want to say something about it in a moment. I want to say to our diplomatic and political friends at the present time the danger is that if anything there will be a little too much caution. Hesitation, delay and undue cautiousness may cause us to lose valuable opportunities for building peace.
May I leave off there, Mr. Chairman, and call it six o'clock?

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

At six o'clock I was remarking that while we should exercise every caution, we should beware lest our policy is too slow, too cautious. I think perhaps that is one criticism that might be made of the-president's otherwise excellent speech, that he seemed to expect the initiative to come' from the other side. I think we should do-everything we possibly can to seize and retain the initiative ourselves as far as possible. There should be no reason why we should wait for all the steps to be taken by the communists.
We know, of course, how disappointing previous negotiations and efforts to reach satisfactory settlements of particular issues have been through the years. Let me give an example. I believe there have been some 257 meetings in an effort to conclude an Austrian peace treaty. This, of course, indicates the difficulty. I think that, though our negotiators may be weary, we should not miss any opportunities if there seem to be any prospects for a settlement. I hope there are more prospects for a settlement today than there were.
I want to say something about the specific steps that might be taken. First of all, of course, there is the necessity of concluding a Korean armistice. May I say that at noon today the radio carried reports appearing in the British press. They, like many of us, are frankly disturbed by what appears to be the rather truculent attitude of the United States military negotiators. We in this group have repeatedly urged that these negotiations be carried on by civilian representatives of the

The demand for such a change is now being made by many others, including such well-informed and responsible newspapers as the Manchester Guardian. While that may be very slow, I think every effort should be made to bring the negotiations to a successful conclusion. We must not allow the talks to break down on questions of detail concerning the mechanics we should use in giving effect to the principles that might be decided upon. I have been a bit disturbed lately by some articles and statements that have been appearing in the United States press. I think it is particularly important that the question of an armistice in Korea should not be tied up with the situation in Indo-China. There have been suggestions by some leaders in the United States that a settlement in Korea should be conditional upon a settlement in Indo-China.
I believe it would be the height of folly to tie these two problems together at the present time, because they are not similar situations.
In Korea there was an act of aggression by one separately constituted government against another government, and the government that was the subject of the aggression was a government which we recognized and was recognized internationally. It was clearly a threat to international security. I believe the United Nations had no option but to take the action that was taken at that time. However, that was not the case with regard to Indo-China. Indo-China is a colonial area and the primary issue is whether French colonialism is going to be strengthened in its attempt to maintain its control over the natives of Indo-China. For some time now I have held the view that this whole issue should be settled by the United Nations, and settled in a manner that would give as much independence as possible to the area and would undertake to assist the people in economic rehabilitation.
In an editorial just three days ago the Christian Science Monitor wisely sums up the situation so far as the United States is concerned by pointing out that the United States must recognize, and I quote:
-that unless American aid is used to promote Indo-Chinese independence rather than to defend French prerogatives, it might as well be stopped tomorrow.
I think that is a consensus which is very widely held. As I have said, the first step in building peace must be the conclusion of a Korean armistice, a very difficult thing to


do. I think every attempt should be made to bring about that armistice.
In the second place, I believe the western leaders should offer in good faith to negotiate a settlement of other outstanding issues in the Far East. This will involve the removal of nationalist China from the United Nations and the recognition of the new regime in China. If a Korean armistice is agreed upon in the negotiations leading up to such a peace, the very fact that the new government of China was one of the negotiating nations would involve a degree of recognition. I believe that Formosa should be taken over as a United Nations trusteeship, and not given back to the Chinese communists or placed under the control of Chiang Kai-shek. It should be taken over by the United Nations trusteeship council until such time as the wishes of the Formosan people as to their future status can be properly determined.
Thirdly, I would urge our government to make every effort toward the reopening of negotiations on the unification of Germany. This is probably the most important issue in the world, including the Far Eastern questions I have been discussing. Every effort should be made to obtain Russia's agreement. The primary consideration, of course, must be free elections-and completely free 

as the first step towards unification and the taking of further steps towards the independence of that country. Divided as she is at the present time, Germany is a festering sore in the heart of Europe and one which, as we all know from long and very bitter experience, can be extremely dangerous to the peace of the whole world. It is vital to both Russia and the west that an agreed solution be found for this extremely grave German problem.
Then in the fourth place we should offer to sit down again with the Russians in the hope of negotiating, as I have already said, an Austrian peace treaty. Even though we have had 257 meetings, we should be ready now to hold the 258th, particularly since there is now some hope that the truculence of the Soviet union which previously stood in the way of agreement may be perhaps a bit softened.
Fifth, we should ask for a reopening of discussions on arms limitation and the control of atomic energy. I think we are all interested in that particular phase. One of the references in President Eisenhower's speech of April 16, to which I have already referred several times, which evoked the best response all over the world, both in the western world and in Russia, was this statement:
-this government is ready to ask its people to join with all nations in devoting a substantial percentage of the savings achieved by disarmament to a fund for world aid and reconstruction ... to help

other peoples to develop the underdeveloped areas of the world . . .
That was one of the most statesmanlike statements the President of the United States has yet made. There could be no more humane alternative to the present state of affairs which causes natural resources and human brains and energy to be harnessed to the production of weapons of war and destruction.
The president dwelt on the stupendous costs of armaments and revealed what equivalent sums of money could do in the way of producing the essentials of life. Those of us who heard the speech, I think, were struck with the numerous examples he gave. Nothing illuminates more clearly the inhumane and inhuman direction of world affairs than when we reflect on the fact that the cost of one heavy bomber is robbing the world of more than 30 modern schools; or two electric power plants, each plant to serve a city of 60,000 people; or two hospitals; or fifty miles of concrete pavement. I think that was one of the most striking illustrations the president gave, although he gave others; namely that the cost of one heavy bomber is eating up what might otherwise be used to bring health, education, sanitation, transportation and so on to the peoples of the world.
So it is that I say: Let us follow up President Eisenhower's lead in this respect at least and try, if we possibly can, to reopen negotiations on these questions; and if possible, let our side seize the initiative. I think we should make every endeavour to try to secure Russian and Chinese co-operation in a general diversion of the money now spent on arms to the rehabilitation as well as to the constructive development of countries and areas around the world without distinction as to political control or colour. Indeed that would be the only way, I think, that such a plan could be placed in operation.
Furthermore we might propose a general conference to explore the possibility of expanding trade between east and west. I agree entirely with what my friend the hon. member for Peel said this afternoon when he was discussing this problem. There is nothing of more vital concern to the democratic countries than the reopening of the channels of trade. If we fail to do that our economies may become undermined and the tactics of the Soviet union with regard to trade and commerce may prove to be far more effective than any propaganda in the cold war and indeed the use of arms in a hot war. I would therefore urge that we ourselves as Canadians, through our Department of External Affairs, our Minister of Trade and Commerce and others, make every effort to
Supply-External Affairs unblock the channels of trade and give the world an opportunity to build an economic structure that will withstand any blows that may come from any direction.
Finally, it may be worth while to try to stop the kind of political warfare we have had over the past few years. Those of us who have been at the United Nations and have heard the speeches there realize how intense this political warfare has been. I think little has been gained by the bitter criticisms that have been made by both sides; and when I say this, I am not in any way forgetting that the bitter speeches were initiated by the Soviet union and the satellite countries under its control. There is no way of knowing at this point whether progress towards peace can be secured along all or even along any of the lines I have been suggesting. I am merely discussing this matter in order to set us thinking about some of these problems. Like others, I am not sure that we would be successful but let us, if we can, seize the initiative. Then we may have an opportunity of bringing some light into the present darkness. But the point I want to emphasize as strongly as I can is that no opportunity should be lost for want of trying.
I also want to say quite clearly and distinctly, as I did at the outset of my remarks this afternoon, that we do not for one moment suggest that we should let down our guard. The soviets may not be sincere. This may not be a change in policy at all but merely a change in tactics. We do not know. Consequently we must not let down our guard. This whole peace offensive may be deliberately designed to induce the west to slow down its military rearmament. We must not do that. We must not abandon the principle of collective security. We must safeguard our own defences and the defences of those with whom we are co-operating in NATO. We must maintain our armed strength until there is provision for general disarmament through the United Nations; world-wide collective security, with all the necessary safeguards of inspection and control; and an international police force operating under the direction of the United Nations and in accordance with international law. This will take time. But until that is done, we must not be induced by any stratagem or trick into lowering our military defences.
But as I have already stressed, on the diplomatic and political fronts, as distinct from the military front, there is not the same necessity for this kind of slow, cautious approach. A new opportunity is opening before us, I believe. We should act upon it with boldness, imagination and sincerity in the hope that if successful agreements with the communists can be reached, the deadly

Supply-External Affairs horror of mankind marshalled into two armed camps and marching to atomic catastrophe will be lifted from the world.
I wanted to place. these views before the Secretary of State for External Affairs, Mr. Chairman, because I know they are quite widely shared. While we must not in any sense weaken our side, nevertheless we should endeavour to seize the initiative as far as negotiations are concerned and try to bring about understandings at least that will give the world a breathing space from this sort of nightmare that hangs over us at the present time.
After all, Canada is sometimes said to be among the smaller nations; but again, those of us who have been at the United Nations know that Canada is very generally respected and trusted by other countries. Our country, because it is influential, could perform a very useful function in speaking out when it is necessary to speak out and urging the great powers on our side to get the initiative in their hands and endeavour to bring about at least a period of armistice and of peace.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I hope some of the matters will be considered and that some good may come from Canada's efforts along lines similar to those I have suggested.

Mr. Chairman, I am afraid I must weary my fellow members of the house almost unbearably because I continually insist on emphasizing technique. What is the use of talking about what ought to be when you do not show how to bring it into being? We have heard speeches in this debate telling us things we already know. For example, "we shall have to remove the blocks to trade". Well, every 14 year old child in Canada knows that, but the thing he does not know is how on earth to do it. It seems to me that is the thing hon. members should be busying themselves talking about; how to do it.
While the talks were going on in 1944 and 1945, while we were arguing Dumbarton Oaks, the Bretton Woods agreement and the San Francisco conference proposals, I think I said over and over again there was no use in trying to remove wars until you first remove the cause of war. The fundamental cause of war is adverse trade balances, or the fear of adverse trade balances. If we will go to work to remove the danger of adverse trade balances and will discover how to accomplish that end, we shall not need any United Nations or Bretton Woods or ITO or any of the other alphabetical monstrosities with which we have been afflicted now for ten years.
The big question is, how can we accomplish all of this? First, I should say the problem is
[Mr. Coldwell-I
one of distribution. I know a great many people can glibly say: Our problem is one of distribution; we have solved the problem of production. True; and that is one of the main causes of our embarrassment of the present moment and our intense peril at the present moment, that we have learned how to produce more than we know what to do with, but we have not learned how to distribute it. Therefore I would urge upon the minister in the first place that from now on he devote his full attention to trying to find out how to solve the problem of maldistribution. Then, I believe all the other things will take care of themselves.
I am going to ask the minister several rather pointed questions to find out for the country just what he does at the United Nations, not only out in the front, but back in the corridors behind the curtains when he talks with people, what he tells people ought to be done to make right the wrongs of this world. I would like to ask the minister several questions and make a few comments, and I should like him to answer these questions before he concludes this debate, because I believe the country has a right to his answers. The first question is: Has the minister urged upon the United Nations the vital importance of increasing the production of food all over the world, including Canada and the United States and offshore territories including Cuba?
Ask the Minister of Agriculture.

I think probably I know something about whom to talk to. What is the use of the Minister of Agriculture increasing the production of food when he cannot sell it, and the increased production results in a fall in the price of food to the producers? That is a rather superficial comment, I think.
According to the figures which I have, and which the minister will check with me, the world's food production, since world war II concluded, has increased only 9 per cent, while the world's population has increased 13 per cent. Is that in accordance with the minister's information also? This information came from an article which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of March 26, 1953, by Gove Hambidge, who I understand is a prominent figure in the United Nations organization. If those figures are correct, and I am pretty sure they are, then obviously this matter of increasing food production is of the most serious concern; yet the nations which are increasing food production are finding themselves embarrassed in the extreme because they are unable to sell profitably. It is estimated that 1,400 million people in the world go to bed hungry every

night. The minister will check with me as to whether that is an extravagant statement. It is correct as far as I have been able to ascertain.
The next question I wish to ask the minister is: Has he urged upon the United Nations the compelling necessity of devising a means of getting North American surpluses into the hands of the starving millions in less favoured lands? For if these surpluses are not put into the hands of the people who need them, we are creating the makings of disaster both among the less favoured peoples and among our own people where we are increasing food production. Therefore I ask the minister, has he urged upon the United Nations this vital matter, so that instead of spending too much time arguing with the Russians at Panmunjon and elsewhere, they might urge something practicable to relieve, if not end, the strains in the world? I have a quotation from the Rlberta wheat pool budget of April 10, 1953, which I believe will help to emphasize the importance of what I have just said:
Problems of parity
With billions of dollars tied up in farm commodities under the current parity price support program, the United States administration is now in a serious dilemma. Lack of export demand is piling up surpluses. Acreage reduction may be put into effect in 1954 if this year's crop turns out to be a big one. About $1,650 million is involved in stocks of wheat, corn and cotton now in government hands. Another $100 million is in dairy products.
Wheat farmers could place their wheat under government loan. The loan price was around $2,20 basis the farm until January 31. Some 455,800,000 bushels from the 1952 crop is so impounded, with an investment of government money of about $1,000 million. The year-end carryover, estimated at 550 million bushels, may be all in government custody.
About $300 million is invested in cotton and $350 million in corn under the same conditions.
That must impress upon the minister, if he needs to have it impressed upon him, the urgent necessity of devising means whereby these surpluses can be put into the hands of the 1,400 million starving people.
Too many people think such distribution can be accomplished by trade; but if Britain, France, Germany, Japan and other nations , are unable to trade with the United States because they cannot get United States dollars, how in the name of common sense can you expect less favoured peoples in these unhappy lands to get United States dollars? If they are unable to get United States dollars how can they possibly procure the surpluses available in the United States which are simply crying to be used?
I asked first whether the minister had urged upon the United Nations the need for 68108-305
Supply-External Affairs increasing food production. Let me bring to the attention of the committee and of the minister, whose mind undoubtedly has been occupied with other matters to the exclusion of things like this, what has been happening to people in the world who have sought to increase the production of food. In 1952 Cuba increased her production of sugar from 5,000,000 tons to 8,000,000 tons. Inasmuch as she was contributing toward increasing the food supplies of the world, Cuba must have been performing a service of the first magnitude to the unhappy peoples of the world. But what happened to Cuba? She found that the price of sugar fell from around 8 cents per pound to around 4 cents per pound. That was the reward Cuba received for her virtuous act in contributing to the supply of food available to nourish the 1,400 million starving people.
Surely it must be obvious to the minister and every member of this committee and every person in the country that if we reward virtue in increasing production in a manner such as that, we are not going to get increased production. In the article which I read concerning the United States situation in respect of food surpluses, we find the suggestion that in all probability next year the United States will take land out of production, which will be directly decreasing the amount of food and will constitute a disservice to the whole world, including the less favoured peoples who are going to bed hungry every night. I think the minister will now see what is behind that question.
The next question I wish to ask the minister is this. What specific suggestions as to techniques has the minister made to the members of the United Nations? By this I mean techniques for transmitting surpluses from the surplus-producing lands to the needy people in the less favoured lands. Has he made any suggestions at all? If he has not made any suggestions, what contribution to the solution of this problem has been made? Is that all his being present at the United Nations means?
I dare venture to suggest that the major single problem confronting the world today is this problem of getting surpluses from some countries into the hands of needy people. If we do not take care of the needy people we run the risk of communism spreading like prairie fire all over the world. If we fail to get the surpluses from the people who produce too much we run the risk of depression in those countries and again spreading communism far and wide, even right in our own country. So I ask, has the minister offered any techniques? To be more specific,

Supply-External Affairs
where has he proposed the money is to come from to go to FAO so that FAO will be able to take the surpluses and distribute them, as it was originally designed to do when it was first set up?
The next question I wish to ask categorically is: Has the minister noticed how gravely inadequate as a means of distribution ordinary international trade is becoming? I have stood completely astonished during my 17 years in this house at the nonchalant manner in which members of the house assume that everything can be settled by international trade. That was implied in both the major speeches we had this afternoon. "Just free the trade blocks!" "It is simple as ABC." "Nothing to it." And everything will follow. That is a most immature approach to the problem. I am tempted to call it irresponsible, except that I know the hon. gentlemen and know that they are just two of many who are like themselves.
Let me now indicate some of the inadequacies which are developing in international trade and becoming more dangerous every year because of the rapid development of machines, technological skills and the use of solar energy which is characteristic of our day.
In the first place, we find that some nations are tending to become almost self-sufficient, as the United States has done. That is the reason United States dollars are so hard to obtain. It is not the result of any perversity on the part of the United States people; it results from the fact that they desire to produce their own. That is something which they have a perfect right to do.
Canada is developing rapidly in the same direction, and there are other units that probably are capable of doing a similar thing. Every nation that becomes self-sufficient practically eliminates itself from the possibilities of trade because it is unable to accept goods into its economy and therefore it is unable in accordance with the principles of orthodox trade to send goods out. The United States is seeking to solve the problem in her own case by burdening herself almost unbearably with mutual aid, foreign spending, foreign credits and so on, all of which result in putting the recipient nations in debt to the United States, putting them under obligations to the United States and generally contributing to the complexity of the whole situation.
This is the first movement or trend which is tending to decrease the possible efficiency of international trade as a means of international distribution.

The next factor-it is not exactly a trend- is the fact that there are many economies which are weak. Take Cuba as an example. Cuba is relatively speaking a one-crop country. She has to protect her economy with utmost rigour; otherwise there would come pouring into her markets goods which would utterly destroy her economy and throw her into an adverse trade balance such as she would never survive. There are many nations in a more or less similar position. As we all know, even Canada is not free from that sort of difficulty..
The third consideration is that, for one reason or another, many nations are unwise in their trade negotiations. The result is that they incur serious adverse trade balances. Our own Canada is an example of that, as we all know. We have an over-all favourable balance of trade, but we have an adverse balance of trade with the United States that is an ever-present danger to us, while we have a favourable balance of trade with Great Britain and other countries, and we find it difficult to use the credits derived therefrom.

This illustrates another difficulty which stands in the way of international trade. When full wisdom dawns in the minds of those who manage Canada and the Canadian people, they will not do things like this; although, I grant they will complicate the trade situation for the United States very much, because many markets which she relies upon in Canada will be cut off from her. But Canada will be trading with the British commonwealth, which will be advantageous to them and to us, also, because we will have obtained goods, and we will not have had an adverse trade balance with the United States.
A situation similar to this that we find in Canada has developed in the economies of a great many nations of the world, and is causing them no small amount of concern.
The fourth trend which is cause for much alarm is that the United States, through her tremendous productive potential, is penetrating and monopolizing world markets. This she is doing, first, by competition, because she has such tremendous productive capacity, with such an enormous market in her own home country, that she is able to produce enough of given commodities to enable her producers to pay their way and make a profit, so they can market their remaining goods in the economies of other nations at competitive levels sufficient to enable the United States to drive out other goods in those other economies. That is not imaginary. It actually happens. The United States is doing this.
Then she is making a tremendous number of advances to other nations. When she is making these advances, in large measure she is making them in the form of her Point Four

Supply-External Affairs program advances. This means, for example, that in country ABC the United States will place United States tractors. She will lend money with which to buy the tractors, making advances to country ABC. Then that country, because it has purchased United States-type tractors, will be under the necessity of buying her repairs from the United States. This means that the country has become tied to, and obligated to, the United States in a way which more or less gives the United States a monopoly on that country's trade.
This matter is of tremendous seriousness at the present time, dangerous not only to Canada but to many other nations in the world including Great Britain, Germany, France, and other nations who would like to trade with countries whose markets the United States is more or less binding to herself by her foreign aid grants. Just to show how great these advances by the United States are I have an excellent statement here which I can vouch for. Mr. Chairman, before the minister answers, I have something to add to the questions of the hon. gentleman. It is a translation of an article which was published in "Carteles" of Havana, April 19, 1953. It is an appropriate article because it is entitled "Mentes agiles in accion", which means "Alert minds in action". What I have in my hand is a French translation, and I shall do my best to translate it into English.
In a certain Spanish-American country they were having economic difficulties. The revenues were decreasing and it was impossible to balance the budget. The cabinet met in session to find some way of fixing up the public finances.
Suddenly the minister of labour rose and gave a bang on the table. He said, "I have found out what to do. We will declare war on the United States". "On the United States?" said the president, who was extremely worried when being told of such an absurd proposal. "If you repeat it, I will have you shot." "No, my dear president; you have not understood", said the minister of labour. "Let us examine recent history. Germany declared war on North America and lost. Then what happened? The United States has given Germany machines, food and money. What happened in the case of Italy? Italy declared war on North America, and we know what happened. Today Italian industry is prosperous. Thousands of Yankee tourists travel in Italy, and there is a great deal of United States money over there. What happened with regard to Japan? Japan took the United States by surprise, lost the war, and now they have good markets, good friends and a balanced budget with Uncle Sam's dollars. I am not crazy. If we declare war on the United States we will become a prosperous country."
This argument made a great impression and convinced the other ministers. Everybody spoke at the same time and the enthusiasm was delirious. "Gentlemen", said the president, "shall I declare war? I will." "Well, Mr. President", said the minister of finance who had been silent until then, "We will declare war; but before doing so, I should like someone to answer this simple question. What will happen if, instead of losing the war, we win it?"

It now seems perfectly obvious that this new drive into Laos is part of a plan to set up in that part of southeast Asia a communist puppet republic which would probably include parts of Burma, Thailand, Laos and Viet Nam. Apparently just a short time ago the red

Supply-External Affairs
Chinese government formed in southeast Asia a puppet regime which they have called the "autonomous government of the Thai nationalities of Yunnan". Reports indicate that the capital of this new state is to be Cheli, in China's Yunnan province only about 50 miles from where China's borders meet the frontiers of Burma and Laos.
It is now evident that if such a puppet state is set up, it would be based on the one common language. Apparently this language, which is known as the Thai language, is common to the people in the border areas of all those states which I have mentioned and this would appear to be a plan to establish in southeast Asia a new country from which attacks could be made on the other nations in that area which are now on our side, either by way of direct armed intervention or by propaganda. It is also evident that there are fifth columnists in all of those free nations. The situation is therefore extremely serious.
So serious is it that 1 week ago in the United States statements were made to the effect that foreign aid which was meant for Europe might be diverted to Indo-China. I have here a dispatch from Washington of April 28, and we find Secretary of State Dulles quoted as follows:
Secretary of State Dulles told the Senate foreign relations committee that communist aggression now centred against Laos had "created a serious new problem which disturbs all peace-loving peoples".
Tim chairman of the senate foreign relations committee, Senator Wiley of Wisconsin, had this to say:
Senator Wiley said Dulles had taken the gravest view of the position in Indo-China and had described that area as presently "the world's most dangerous spot".
I believe that to be an accurate summing up of the situation. I would ask the minister to tell us what the opinion of the government is with regard to this particular situation. On December 30 of last year the Canadian government recognized Viet Nam, Laos and Cambodia as associated states of Indo-China within the French union in accordance with the terms of agreement between France and the respective states. I am reading from the report of the minister's department. I believe that Canada could do something to help this situation. Take, for example, the possibility of Canada helping with transport planes. Apparently the United States is doing that. Is Canada prepared to render any assistance?
Is Canada prepared further to take any steps to bring order into the relations of the freedom-loving nations in the Pacific area?
I was much impressed by a statement made by Field Marshal Montgomery before the

national press club in the United States just a few weeks ago. He was invited there by the leading United States reporters, and one of them asked him about the situation in the Pacific. This was his reply:
If you want to boil me down to one point, which I suppose you do, I would say the real thing that's necessary is political guidance from the politicians.
He was referring to the Pacific. He went on:
That's what is wanted. And there isn't any. There isn't any. If you gentlemen can tell me what is the agreed political aim in the Far East, I'll be very glad to know it. I can't tell you the answer to that and you can't tell me-there isn't one. And it's absolute nonsense. What's the good of going on in this damn silly way? Let's get political guidance from the politicians. Is that clear?
I believe that Canada could help to give some political guidance in affairs across the Pacific. As the minister knows, I have urged upon him at different times that Canada should take part in the treaties affecting the Pacific. I have asked him time and again vhy Canada Is rot a part" to the treaty Detween Australia, new Zealand and the United States, which is known as the ANZUS treaty. On each occasion I have been given what might accurately be termed the brush-off. Just a few days ago the New Zealand minister of external affairs explained why Canada is not a party to that treaty. I have been told here in the house on each occasion, I think, that Canada had not been invited. Then I would ask: well, if she is invited what will she do, will she accept or will she decline? To that I have always had the answer: We shall have to decide that when we are invited. But the minister of external affairs of New Zealand gave the show away the other day. He was being badgered in the house by one of the opposition members about why Canada was not a party to this ANZUS treaty, and finally he said:
Canada didn't want to be In, that's the explanation.
I am quoting from a press dispatch of April 21, 1953.
At some time there has to be an organization set up to co-ordinate the actions of the different freedom-loving nations in the Pacific area. We have such an organization in the Atlantic; but in the Pacific, as Field Marshal Montgomery says, nobody knows what the politicians want. Every nation is going in a different direction. I do hope that our Secretary of State for External Affairs will be more favourable tonight to the suggestion that Canada should not only ask to become a party to this ANZUS treaty, but should throw her weight behind the idea of setting up some kind of an organization in the Pacific which will be able to hold the communist

threat, as we are doing successfully in the Atlantic area.
Here we have this move into Laos, which is part of the large picture. No one knows what the next move will be. If they do succeed in starting trouble in Thailand and in Burma, it will probably also work down into Malaya and all our chances of straightening out the situation in that very dangerous area may well be gone. I would hope that the Canadian government would be willing now to take some steps to help bring about an organization in the Pacific area which could meet this situation.
I was just wondering whether the hon. member who has just taken his seat would be prepared to support a measure of taxation in Canada to take on the responsibility emanating from his suggestion.

That question is really not a very sensible one. Actually, if we had an organization in the Pacific such as we have in the Atlantic, in the long run it would save this country not only millions of dollars but the lives of a great many young Canadians.

Mr. Chairman, though I was a little discouraged a few minutes ago by the remark of the hon. member for Lethbridge when he said in his speech that anything said outside government ranks was about as effective as the bleating of a lamb in a blizzard-I hope he was exaggerating-at any rate, I am going to bleat for a few minutes.
I noted that the hon. member for Peel, followed by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, referred to the question of trade; and that carried my mind back to something that occurred in this house a few days ago on the agriculture estimates when the question of sales abroad was discussed, and the Minister of Agriculture said that actually when it came to this question it was more a matter for the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I thought that was a very fair statement for the Minister of Agriculture to make. I was hoping that the minister of external affairs might have had something more to say about it today. It is true that he made a short speech and mentioned other things verging on the question of trade, but I do not think he really addressed his mind to trade at all.
There was a remark made in this house the other day by the hon. member for Lake Centre which I thought was most significant and I wish to deal with it, along with the ideas which emanated from it, because it seems to me that we have a situation of the very greatest gravity. Although
Supply-External Affairs we as Canadians must not take ourselves too seriously, nevertheless we should take ourselves seriously enough.
The point made was that just as in wartime economic and military efficiency were regarded as two sides of the same shield, so should that be the case today. I should like to refer the committee briefly to the Hyde Park agreement of 1941 and read just a sentence from the words of the prime minister at that time. I quote:
At Hyde Park on April 20, 1941, the Prime Minister of Canada and the President of the United States agreed "as a general principle that in mobilizing the resources of this continent, each country should provide the other with the defence articles which it is best able to produce, and above all, produce quickly,-''
What seems more significant than that to me was the exchange of notes which took place in 1945 at the end of the period of actual fighting. This was an exchange of notes between Ray Atherton and the acting secretary of state for external affairs, the present Minister of National Defence, and I quote:
In view of the high degree of economic interdependence of the Canadian and American economies, the government of the United States desires to assure the government of Canada that it will consider and deal with the problem of the transition from war to peace in the spirit of the Hyde Park declaration which gave rise to such successful co-operation for war purposes.
Although it is hard for us to realize it, I suggest that we are in a position today where this co-operation is almost if not quite as important as it was four or five years ago. The importance may be concealed. We may be apt to forget, although we should not in the light of what has been said here today and the light, I am sure, of what the minister said and will say as to the grim possibilities of the situation and the duties which lie on all of us.
Trade is so much harder than aid. Aid appeals to the generosity of people and their kinder instincts. Other things are brought in which we have seen operate in a big way. But when it comes to trade, that is infinitely harder. Then you have people's self-interest entering into the thing. I should like to read two short extracts which I believe point out what I consider to be an acute and important situation at the moment. Those of us who rejoiced at the election of President Eisenhower but who knew that the traditional Republican attitude might make it difficult for him when it came to trade, unfortunately now have a great deal of reason to fear that he may be frustrated in certain ways. If it is still respectable to do so I should like to read briefly from the Globe and Mail. This is the Globe and Mail itself, and not a quotation of somebody else. This is from the

Supply-External Affairs column by Wellington Jeffers who was reporting on a talk he had had with a man in Washington. The name is not given. This is what that man said to him:
There never was so much imagination, know-how about the large movement of trade and practical ability at the top as now. I tremble because, at the same time, there never were more hidebound members at the lower levels of politics insisting on all sorts of duties and regulations whose results would be, if followed, to sew up the world trade worse than it was sewed up in the early 30's.
That was a statement by a very serious man. Now I should like to read just a sentence or two from the New York Times of May 3. This is entitled "Gloomy Outlook Seen for Exports". I quote:
The big debate in Washington was centred primarily on legislation to expand the reciprocal trade agreements act due to expire on June 12. The house ways and means committee devoted its first week of hearings to witnesses favouring a considerable tightening of the law to avert supposedly "disastrous" effects of a rise in imports.
That underlines what was said a few minutes ago by the hon. member for Lethbridge as to the terrible difficulties and the great danger of world trade not merely not improving but worsening. It is comforting to read the next paragraph from this same New York Times as follows:
The United States chamber of commerce, on the other hand, at its convention in the national capital adopted a resolution strongly favouring "trade, not aid" and called for the reduction of import barriers so that foreign nations could earn needed dollars.
I need not do more than remind the committee of the disastrous effect that could have on the gallant and I hope successful attempts being made by the British under the leadership of Mr. Butler, chancellor of the exchequer, to break loose from restrictions and try to step back into a far greater measure of freedom. I should like to read just a few words from the Economist of April 18, page 131, where they refer to the budget proposals in the following words:
Whatever criticisms may be made of their details, they have the great recommendation that they mark a determination to "step out from the confines of restriction to the almost forgotten but beckoning prospects of freer endeavour and greater reward for effort."
We all remember that in spite of all the difficulties they are facing in Britain, the adoption of a courageous attitude a year ago has improved things. They are moving forward, but nevertheless the attitude of the United States, as we all know, is going to be absolutely vital. We must hope, and I think we are entitled to hope, that results will flow from the visit made a month or so ago by Butler and Eden; but the fact is that when they got back to England they were very cautious in anything they were able to say.

The people in England had the feeling that not very much that was definite had been accomplished.
I should like to refer briefly to an article in Foreign Affairs of April, 1953 by a writer who has a high standing in the United States. This man has been in official positions and is chairman of the General American Investors Company, and vice-president and secretary of the council on foreign relations. He evidently represents a good combination of a businessman and an international expert. What he refers to in this article was mentioned earlier in the committee, that there is a great possibility that this new look on the part of the Russians may be for the purpose of lulling us into a sense of security and prompting the breaking down of our own economic organizations.
He quotes from an article written by Stalin some time ago in which the Russian dictator spoke most confidently about what he called "the disintegration of the single all-embracing world market". Stalin then went on to make the most gloomy predictions about what was going to happen to the free world, or, as he called it, the capitalist system. I am not going to read this at length, but I do suggest that we face clearly the realities of the situation, which I think are that if in fact the free world is not going to find a way to co-operate, then the gloomy predictions of Stalin as to our future may very well become true.
What mode of co-operation would be possible among the countries of the world? I suggest that the mode of co-operation is that which would develop the means of trading with each other. I do not take the gloomy view taken by the hon. member for Lethbridge that it is not possible that we can develop freer channels of trade, but it would be a very foolish and blind man who would deny that at the present time there are a great many very disquieting circumstances indeed.
That leads me to one further comment I wish to make, and that is that if it is correct to say-and I believe it is-that it is vital to the welfare of all of us that the United States shall be able to take a co-operative attitude-if we agree that that is vital, I say, then it is incumbent upon us not merely to bring to bear on her all the influence we have, but also to do what we can do ourselves. We are not the United States; nevertheless we have a very substantial trade of our own, and we can play an important part.
When we look back 13 years to 1940 we realize that, partly by virtue of our geographical position, and also for other reasons, we can say that we played an almost decisive

part. I hope the minister will say something about this, because I believe it is our duty to take ourselves very seriously in this matter again at the present time.
First of all we have to believe, in my view, that this is a matter of vital importance. We have to believe that the United States mutatis mutandis must be prepared to get back into the state of mind it was in seven years ago when the letter from which I read was written, at which time, in 1945, they were ready to co-operate.
And of course if they can be convinced of the seriousness of the situation we may have every reason to believe that they will meet it. On the other hand, if it is allowed to drift, if the attempts the British are making now should fail, there is only one thing that will happen, and that is that the free countries will be thrown back upon a devastating suicidal every man for himself attitude such as prevailed in the thirties, when everyone was pulling himself up by his own boot straps, and when we had trade restrictions at every turn.
It is fashionable now to pretend that that was because of the stupidity of this or that government, or this or that country. But the truth of the matter, as any serious student of the situation in that period must know, is that we had then drifted into a situation following the first world war where it was a case of the devil take the hindmost and where each nation believed in the pursuit of the immediate objective.
That is a situation which, I suggest, we should not believe is infinitely remote at this time; and anything that can be done by the government to prevent it, is important and urgent.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think I owe it to the committee to try in a few words to deal with some of the points which have been raised during the course of the debate. I shall have a word to say first about the statements of the hon. member for Peel, who put to me some concrete questions on specific subjects.
He brought up, for instance, arising out of the report of the standing committee, the question as to the need for economy in the management of our foreign service, and in the construction of foreign service buildings abroad. I agree of course with everything he said on that matter. And the example which he quoted to show the need for this caution was an item in the estimates for the construction of an embassy building in Rome. This item, as he put it, was for the sum of three-quarters of a million dollars, including the price of the land.
Supply-External Affairs
On that all I wish to say, by way of explanation, is that this amount comes out of blocked funds which we got as the result of an agreement we made with the government of Italy. But in the use of those funds we should employ the same methods of economy and good business as we would use in the case of our own dollars. We try to adopt exactly the same principles of control. But it is also true that it is normally more economical and also better business in the management of a foreign service to own property abroad than to rent it; because when renting we lose the advantage of immunity from taxation, rates, and things of that kind, that we get by owning the property. And so when we got this blocked lira in Italy we looked around for land in which to invest it; because in a period of rising prices and threatening inflation, land is a better investment for your money than bank notes.
Thus we bought land, and have placed in the estimates a sum of money for the possible construction during this year of a Canadian building in Rome, which would include not only the embassy residence but the chancellery and office accommodation for all Canadian activities there. But I can assure the committee that that building will not be constructed during this year or during any year in which I happen to be responsible for the Department of External Affairs, unless it is good business so to do. I put this amount in the estimates this year, but it does not by any means indicate that the building will necessarily be constructed during this financial year. It was to provide for the possibility of making a good deal during the year that this amount of blocked funds was put in the estimates.
The hon. member also spoke about the necessity for close liaison with the C.B.C. international service. Of course we agree with that and, as he knows, we have taken steps in the last two or three months to make that liaison closer and more useful to all departments concerned.
He brought up the question of passports. I believe the hon. member knows very well the position of the government in that matter. Normally we do not interfere with the right of a Canadian citizen to possess a passport. However, if the activities of that Canadian abroad constitute an immediate danger to the security of the state, we have the right not only to refuse a passport, but to ask for the return of one that that person might have in his possession. We have done that in the past, and we will not hesitate to do it again in the future. But unless these activities do constitute an immediate danger to security, I suggest that we would do well to follow the

Supply-External Affairs practice they have followed in the United Kingdom for so many years, under which normally they do not interfere with a person's right to hold a certificate of identity of this kind.
This brings to mind the tolerant attitude that was so graphically expounded by Mr. Churchill in the House of Commons in London in connection with the activities of the Dean of Canterbury. That attitude I think was a wise one, and normally we follow it in so far as the possession of passports by Canadians is concerned. There is nothing these Canadians who do so much mischief abroad would like more than to be martyred or publicized. And I think when they do not constitute an immediate danger to the state, if we just leave them to themselves, they will soon discredit themselves, and all that Canadians will feel for them will be the contempt they deserve.
The hon. member for Peel made a special point of the usefulness of military attaches in NATO countries. I think I know what he had in mind. He felt probably that in the NATO group of countries, when we have NATO military missions in Paris, and when in those missions we exchange military information, the intelligence functions of military attaches to NATO countries would be duplicated by that exchange of information in Paris.
To some extent that is true. But the intelligence work of an attache-military, naval or air-is only a part of his work. Indeed, in certain NATO countries the work of attaches has increased because of the NATO organization-exchange of troops, negotiations for mutual aid and facilities, and all that sort of thing. So there is no duplication in work, although in some offices abroad in NATO countries it may be that we can reduce some of the military attache work which is taken over by the office in Paris.
Then the hon. member brought up the question of the meaning of recent soviet moves, a subject with which almost every hon. member who has participated in this debate has dealt. The hon. member made reference in this connection to the question of trade. This was mentioned also by the hon. member for Greenwood, who has just taken his seat. In analysing the present position the hon. member for Peel drew our attention, and quite properly, to the danger inherent in an economic situation, by which soviet policy may be directed into trade channels which may be difficult for us to meet. On the face of it these trade approaches may seem to be friendly. They may, however, constitute a problem more difficult than some

of the attacks we have had from that quarter in the past, when we knew where we were and how we could defend ourselves. These trade approaches are now being made, and they are very tempting indeed to countries who have to rely on trade not only for their prosperity but at times for their very existence.
Mention of this possible danger leads me to the other aspect of this trade question. There seems to be now some change from the feeling of a few months ago following the United Kingdom mission to Washington, which in its turn followed the commonwealth conference in London. There was then a feeling of optimism over trade prospects; that we were going to make real progress in the removal of obstacles and limitations, and that we were going to move toward what we call convertibility. Some of that optimism certainly has tended to disappear in recent weeks. There is a relationship between these two aspects of the question. As we of the western world begin to worry more about trade among ourselves, overtures from the other side of the iron curtain become the more tempting, especially to European countries.
It is almost as important at the present time to strengthen rather than weaken our economic co-operation as it is to strengthen our political co-operation. In this connection I do not think I am being unfair to our neighbours to the south when I say that the United States, the most powerful economic and trading nation in the world, the most persistent creditor nation of the world, has a special responsibility in this connection. She has been active in GATT in the past, and no country has benefited more from that activity than Canada.
The United States has shown great generosity in aiding less fortunate countries but, as the hon. member for Greenwood said a few moments ago, we are now entering a period when trade may be more difficult than aid. Trade may be, indeed, a greater test of cooperation within our group of free states than aid itself. Aid has a certain emotional context which makes it possibly easier than is the case with trade. Aid is also spread over the whole taxpaying community; but trade, the removal of limitations on importations, the lowering of barriers and so on, often affects certain groups which have special facilities for making their views known. We may therefore find that while trade and not aid has become the popular slogan at the present time-and it is a good one-it may be one that is very difficult to carry into effect. However, if it is not carried into effect it surely is apparent to all of us that within the

NATO partnership it will be difficult to reconcile political co-operation and economic conflict.
I do not think I am betraying any secret when I say that when the Prime Minister goes to Washington on Thursday this will be one of the subjects, possibly it may be the most important subject, that he will discuss with the President of the United States and his advisers. I have no doubt that we will be able to exchange views on this matter with our friends to the south in the usual frank and friendly way. I hope that as a result of this visit some of our apprehensions-and we all have apprehensions at the present time about the trend of economic events within the NATO community-may be removed.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar in his very interesting and characteristically thoughtful statement analysed for our benefit -I tried to do it in fewer words, and not as effectively as he-what he called the phenomenal change that had taken place at least in some aspects of soviet policy in recent weeks. He cited certain measures, certain words and certain moves to justify the statement that phenomenal changes had taken place. He thought that if we had made a mistake at all in our reaction to these changes, which have certainly taken place, it had been that we were too cautious.
I am not inclined to that view myself. I think while we must be sympathetic and receptive, and not brusque or belligerent, at the same time we should be very cautious indeed. When we were discussing this matter in Paris-possibly I should have gone into this in a little more detail in the beginning- I made a short statement. As it was a more carefully considered statement than the one I gave this afternoon possibly I may be pardoned for reading from it now. I can vouch for the author. I said at that time, and I was almost the last of the speakers:
It seems from the speeches that have been made that we are in unanimous agreement-
I was talking about the NATO council.
-at least on this point; that we do not know whether we are faced with a threat or a promise in recent soviet moves; that while we should exploit anything which may seem to be promising, we certainly should not do this in a way which would leave us weaker if the move turned out to be a threat. There certainly has been no clear pattern in what has recently taken place. We can only make our own interpretations and we should be pretty careful, we all agree, in doing so.
It had been-
. . . pointed out a little while ago-
[DOT]-by one of the earlier NATO speakers-
-that the ultimate objective of soviet policies must be considered as remaining unchanged:	world
domination through communist regimes dependent on Moscow. I am sure we are all agreed that we
Supply-External Affairs
should neither forget that fact, nor be obsessed by it. While the objective may not have changed, tactics, of course, and this is good communist doctrine, have undoubtedly changed. We are not sure of the nature of the change or indeed of its ultimate significance, but we do know that it has taken place, and we are all, of course, asking ourselves 'why'.
After trying to answer some of the questions myself as to why these changes may have taken place, and I shall not repeat that now, I ended with these words:
I think we are all agreed that we should try to bring about as early as possible a recognition of soviet intentions by putting them to a real test. That is being done, I hope, at present in Korea and there are other places in which it might be done. Then there is the necessity of taking every possible action to remove the danger that our public opinions may be mystified and confused and misled by these moves. We should do our best, and possibly NATO can help here, to give the widest possible circulation to the vital distinction between our readiness to negotiate outstanding issues, which we must always emphasize, and our refusal to be deceived by moves which may have been made merely to deceive us. When we say, as we always do say, and quite correctly, I think, that we will meet the Soviet union half-way in these matters or sometimes even more than halfway, it is, I am sure we all agree, wise to keep the initiative in selecting the ground on which we will meet them and to try to discover before we meet them where they are going . . .
This is going to be a difficult problem because the very desire of our peoples for peace is going to make it easier for the soviet at times to raise false hopes. It is not going to be easy to follow the policy of keeping dry an increasing amount of powder, and at the same time, remaining reasonable, unprovocative, pacific in word and in deed.
I am sure that is a policy which commends itself to all sections of the house, because it has been made pretty clear in discussion already that that is the case.
If I had the indulgence of the committee I could finish in about five minutes.
Agreed.

I know the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra would not wish me to sit down without giving him what he is accustomed now to describe as the normal brush-off in respect of a Pacific pact. I have never admitted in the past that that has been our attitude in this important question, and of course I do not admit it now. So I shall once again try to explain to him the policy of the government.
As he pointed out, it is becoming increasingly clear from the events in Indo-China that there is a strategic connection between communist aggression in one part of the world and communist aggression in another. I admit that. It is also a little depressing to compare the peaceful words from Moscow and the aggressive actions in Indo-China. Both-we do not know for sure-may be

Supply

External Affairs directed from the same source. Nevertheless I agree with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar when he says that, though there is a strategic connection between these things which require world military planning, there is a political distinction between the two areas of Korea and Indo-China. We have very definite United Nations obligations in Korea, and I know that our men are fulfilling them there. Especially in the last few days they have been fulfilling them with the kind of courage we expect from Canadian troops. While we are fulfilling our obligations in that way in Korea, we have not the same kind of obligation in Indo-China. I do not think we should be asked to accept that kind of obligation until Indo-China becomes a United Nations matter.
It is open to the French government at any time, or to one of the French union states, to bring this matter to the United Nations if they so desire. As a result of the United Nations action we might find ourselves confronted with exactly the same kind of obligation as Korea, though we might not discharge it in the same way. Until that happens however there is a distinction politically between Indo-China and Korea. I do not say that to minimize the importance of what is going on there, because it would be unwise to do so. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra pointed out certain far-reaching developments which may be taking place in southeastern Asia-the establishment of a new communist satellite state. I am not suggesting, therefore, that this matter may not be important. I am suggesting that there may be a difference between it and Korea.
The hon. member asked quite categorically what we would be willing to do to assist in Indo-China. We will fulfil our obligations as a member of the community of nations, and as a friend of France. I think the French government would be the first to admit that the assistance we have given to France as a member of the NATO association may have helped her recently in the discharge of some of her obligations in Indo-China. But we have not been asked to assist directly in Indo-China, and I have no reason to believe that, until this becomes either a United Nations or a NATO matter in a way which it is not now, we would be asked to do so.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra asked me also quite categorically whether we would take the initiative in joining ANZUS, and if not why not. He has brought this up in every debate on foreign affairs within the last two or three years. I certainly do not criticize him for that, because collective

security in the Pacific is as important as collective security in the Atlantic. But that does not necessarily mean it should be worked out in the same way. He also asks me, as minister for external affairs, whether I would be willing now to take the initiative as the representative of the government in working out a collective security arrangement in the Pacific, as he put it, along the same lines as the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. I can only reply that I think that would be an unwise initiative to take at this time. It seems to me the reason for that is obvious.
It has been made abundantly clear by the United States of America, which has taken the lead in this matter, that in its opinion it would be premature and unwise even to attempt any such arrangement now. If the United States takes that view, and I think under the present circumstances it is the right view, I do not think it would be wise for us to go further and try to take the initiative ourselves. I must deduce from his remarks that he feels-I do not know whether or not he is speaking for his party-that the time is ripe for a Pacific pact with Canada as a member, and that we should accept all the obligations we have accepted under the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. These obligations have resulted in a Canadian brigade being in Europe and twelve squadrons of aircraft as well as many naval ships being added to NATO. But why have we not joined the ANZUS pact? It is not necessarily the kind of special security arrangement in the Pacific to which the hon. member was referring. The ANZUS arrangement is more limited. It includes only Australia, New Zealand and the United States.
Since it does not include any other country, that is one good reason why we are not in it. If it were a wider arrangement, I am quite sure we would very sympathetically consider any invitation to join it. Again, it has been made abundantly clear that those who initiated the arrangement do not wish, at this time, to extend it beyond those three countries. It is well known to members of the house that the United Kingdom has felt a little disturbed and disappointed because she has not been, up to the present, invited to join this arrangement. If the United Kingdom with her far-reaching obligations in the Pacific, territorial and otherwise, and in spite of the feelings of the present government, has not become a member of ANZUS, I think it is not right for the hon. member to say that we have been shirking an invitation or that we have made known in advance that we did not want an invitation and that that is the only reason we have not received one.
I was only quoting the New Zealand minister of external affairs.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I shall let the New Zealand minister speak for himself. I am telling the hon. gentleman that that is not the situation as I understand it. It has been made quite clear to us that it is the desire of the United States government at this time, and the other two governments in ANZUS, not to extend the membership in that association beyond the three countries who are now members. That being the case, surely it would be very bad diplomacy indeed to go scouting around to see if we could get an invitation, or complaining because we had not received one. I assure the hon. member that that is the situation as I see it, and I think I see it accurately.
This does not mean that, in respect of a general Pacific pact, the time may not come when this group should not be extended. If and when that time comes I do not think Canada will shirk her obligations in the Pacific any more than she shirks the discharge of her obligations in other parts of the world. I can only say I hope the hon. gentleman will not think I am brushing off the matter at this time. It is merely that at present we do not think it would be wise or timely to take the initiative, either in respect of a general Pacific pact or of the extension of the existing ANZUS pact.
I believe I have dealt with a good many of the matters that came up during the discussion, Mr. Chairman. The hon. member for Lethbridge asked me a lot of questions,
Supply-External Affairs and I must say I am somewhat relieved that it is after ten o'clock and also that he is out of the chamber. Possibly he will pardon me if I do not answer those questions. I hope some of his friends will tell him that one reason I cannot do so is that I hope the session will end soon, because I then will have the pleasure of paying a visit to his constituency. If I tried to answer the six questions he addressed to me this afternoon, the session would not I fear end for two or three weeks.

Item agreed to.
